COLD STORAGE AND VENTILATION ON OCEAN STEAMERS.
speechtext:
SMITH-by Mr. Taylor-asked :
What was the kind of ventilation, if any, last season, in the compartments in which perishable cargo was stored on the steamers ' Livonia,' ' Tritonia ' and ' Devona ' ; and was the system in proper working order in each such compartment when these steamers left the port of Montreal ?

speechtext:
SS. ' Livonia.'
This vessel did not carry perishable cargo from the Port of Montreal last season.

No. 1 hold :	2 intakes and 1 outtake.

No. 3 hold : 2 intakes and 1 outtake.

SS. ' Devona.'
On this vessel the cold storage and cooled air compartments occupied all the space in the 'tween decks. The holds were ventil-

ated by two steam driven propellor fans, by ten cowl ventilators, and by three trunk ventilators.
The system of ventilation in the steamship ' Tritonia ' and steamship ' Devona ' was on proper working order when these steamers left the port of Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to draw the attention of the House to an article that appears in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of yesterday. The article is not very long and I will read it to the House. It is as follows :	.

Lord Dundonald's Speech at Windsor Banquet. Deplores the interference of politicians with the appointments to the Canadian volunteer force-The condition, he says, is intolerable.
Toronto, June 7.-The 'World' this morning publishes the following sensational story under an Ottawa date :-
A Montreal officer who was present at the military dinner at the Windsor Saturday, stated here to-day that Lord Dundonald's sensational speech, although carefully written out and intended for publication, had been carefully suppressed by the Montreal newspapers.
This is what the general said :
When a nation is in peril the commanding officer had the supreme control of the military appointments, and he is responsible to his country for its efficiency in war. In time of peace, unhappily, through political intriguers, we are in their web, and appointments are made without regard to military efficiency and to the great peril of the nation's safety. Officers in command of the forces of this country should not be selected because of their particular politics, but unfortunately this is the case.
A most flagrant instance of political interference has recently come before me in connection with the appointment of officers in the new eastern townships cavalry regiment, the Scottish Light Dragoons. The commanding officer of the corps had selected officers because of their apparent fitness from a military point of view. The names reached me and were sent to council, and gentlemen, what do you think happened ? The list having my approval was returned with the name of one officer stricken off, and initialed by the Minister of Agriculture.
The gentleman whose name was stricken from the list was Dr. Pickell, the mayor of Sweetsburg, and warden of the county of Mis-sisquoi, a man chosen of the people and well qualified to serve his King and country. His political colour was not, however, that of the Minister of Agriculture, and consequently he was not considered fit to serve his King in the military force of Canada.
' If,' said Lord Dundonald, ' the Hon. Sydney Fisher has been as well versed in soldiering as in agriculture, he would have better understood the responsibilities ot officers, and this would not have happened.'

After making a few more remarks, the general said : ' It is intolerable that my recommendations. made in the best interests of the force, should be so grossly interfered with by any minister, not connected with the department.
Lord Dundonald's speech was greeted with tremendous applause.
Lt.-Col. Whibbard also made a speech in which he endeavoured to shield the Minister of Agriculture, saying that it was difficult to suppose that Hon. Mr. Fisher would be guilty of such an act.
It goes without saying that the speech is the talk of both Ottawa and Montreal.
The question I would like to ask is as to whether the government is aware of this article which is published in the ' Citizen.' It is a very serious matter and I think requires some explanation.

Mr. Speaker, I have to inform my hon. friend from Huntingdon (Mr. Maclaren) and the House as well that the government's attention has been called to the reported speech of Lord Dundonald. The matter is a very grave one and I have only to say that to-morrow the government will be prepared to make a communication to the House upon it.
Why not on Monday ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In answer to the question just put to me by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) why this matter should not be postponed until Monday instead of to-morrow, I would say to my hon. friend that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is under a very serious misapprehension and stricture, and I think it is better that the matter should be cleared up at the earliest possible moment.

The average rate of duty was 18 per cent. What I want to know is, if it is right and proper, and I say it is, that the1 manufacturers of this country should be protected to the extent of 28 per cent, wh y is it not equally right and proper that the farmer, who toils day and night, who earns his money qs hardly as any other people in this country, should also have protection ? I know that hon. gentlemen opposite will

smile and sneer, and say, of what advantage is it to put a duty on wheat, cheese or butter ? Do we not export enormous quantities of these products, and does not the Liverpool price fix the price in Canada ? Then what is the use of putting a duty upon them ? It would not raise the price a single cent. I say if it does not, put it on ; it cannot do anybody any harm. But I fancy if would have the effect of giving the farmers of this country their home market for these $5,756,000 worth of agricultural products which are now imported, instead of their taking the chances of getting their products damaged and spoiled by sending them across the Atlantic. The home market is the best market. Almost everybody will admit that. Hon. gentlemen opposite, who used to sneer at the idea of a home market for the farmers, are now coming to the conclusion that it is their best market. I want to preserve this home market for the farmers, and it can be preserved for them, by giving them as high a duty on their products as is imposed on things they have to buy. That is fair, surely.
Let us discuss some of these items separ-; ately. I want to know why the farmers, of this country cannot supply this market with butter, cheese, lard, pork and grain products. Then, I want to speak of another class of goods that are luxuries. However much we may disagree with hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to other things ; however strong protectionists we may be, and however honestly we may hold our coni victions, however consistent we may have been during the last twenty-five years with regard to protection, and however inconsistent these hon. gentlemen may be in that matter; we can, I believe, all agree on one thing ; protectionists, free traders and revenue tariff men will agree that luxuries should be taxed a little higher than the necessaries of life ; and a large proportion of these agricultural products that come to this country are luxuries, and as such, they ought to pay more than 28 per cent. They ought to pay at least 35 per cent, which is a common rate of duty in our tariff. Just consider that we bring in seventy-nine carloads of these green tomatoes which our market-gardeners around our cities and town could grow. They are a, class of men who are industrious, frugal, persevering and hard working. Our market-gardeners and fruit growers are two classes of men who perhaps earn their money as hardly as any other class in the country. Their productions are subject to droughts, frosts, floods and all manner of insect pests, and they have to be continually on the fight. Theirs is a business that calls forth the highest kind of intelligence, and they are a class of citizens who form the backbone of the great agricultural class. Their life is one that necessarily calls forth the high
est qualities in a man. These men employ a great many men In their business. This government are paying out millions of dollars a year in bonuses.
I think we have paid up to date over $4,000,000 in direct bounties to establish industries in this country. What are these paid for ? Is it not to give employment in this country ? I think that is the great object; and, if so, there is no class among farmers that employ more men than the market-gardeners and fruit growers. They employ ten times the number of men to the square mile that any other class does outside of manufacturers. These are a class of men who ought to be encouraged. They are engaged in an occupation which is particularly hazardous. They ought, therefore, to have at any rate as much protection as is accorded to other industries, namely, 28 per cent. But, as a matter of fact, they are only getting an average of 18 per cent. But the tomatoes I have referred to are luxuries and ought to be subject to a higher duty than the average. They ought to pay 35 per cent or even 45 per cent; but they have to pay only 19J per cent. No wonder the market-gardeners are complaining every year that they are not properly treated by this government. The wonder is that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) has not been more powerful-has not raised his sturdy voice in council and before the Minister of Finance from time to time on! their behalf. I am sure that if the hon. gentleman had raised his influential voice on this question in the manner he has done on other questions, he would have convinced the government that 19i per cent protection is not sufficient for the market-gardener. Go over the various items which the market-gardeners grow, and you will find that the
i.uties are below the average and that these gentlemen have a just grievance against] the government.
I might take up another department ol these agricultural products-the fruit industry. I find that we imported into this country 28,391 barrels of apples, 200 carloads, and exported some 20,000 carloads. No doubt hon. gentlemen opposite will say : if you export in such large quantities, what gcod would it do you to put a higher duty on the small quantity you import ? It would not raise the price a cent. Well, let us have the duty in any case. We will then get the market and that is what our farmers want. What they want is a market at their doors for the 28,000 barrels which they now have to send across the ocean, but which would be consumed at home if these 28,000 barrels of American apples did not come in. They would have that much less to send across in the magnificent cold storage system, of which hon. gentlemen opposite boast so much and to which I shall refer later. Of dried apples we imported no less than eight carloads, and I suppose we had a thousand carloads last', u"year lying upon the ground which went to waste, for a small portion of which this home market might have been preserved. We imported no less than 1,214,239 pounds of cherries and others of those small fruits, which are absolutely luxuries. Turning to the months in which we imported those articles, I find that they were brought in a few days and weeks before our own could be put on the market. But they took the keen edge off the appetites of the consumers of these luxuries. The men who consume these are men well able to pay a little extra duty. I am sure that the hon. the Minister of Finance would not object if there should happen to be a little more money in the treasury. He has a great transcontinental railway scheme on hand, which he will find he will not be able to build for \xa714,000,000. He will find that his surplus of $14,000,000 or $15,000,000 will not be sufficient to build a road which is to cost $150,000,000. He seems to think it will, but in my experience, and I think it is the experience of most business men, when you want to buy a farm, you will not be able to pay for it out of the interest. You will either have to pht down the cash or give a mortgage for the capital sum, and will have to pay the mortgage when it falls due. The hob. minister will find the same thing in the case of his transcontinental line ; and if by raising the duty on those early products, a little more money should go into the treasury, paid by people who can well afford to pay, I am sure he will have no objections. But I am confident a great deal less will come in if the duty is raised, and the keen appetite of the consumers will be preserved for the first products of our own fruit growers and market gardeners. They will be given the opportunity to take advantage of the early market. I may point out that the quality of the fruits produced in Canada is superior to that of any brought a long distance.
Besides these, we also imported no less than 43 carloads of cranberries. Is there any province in the Dominion where we cannot grow cranberries ? We can grow them in every province, yet we have had to import 43 carloads. And of peaches we imported no less than 150 carloads, also 82 carloads of plums, 294 carloads of driend prunes and 150 carloads of other dried fruits, making a total of 444 carloads of dried fruits. Of canned fruits we imported 40 carloads. I want to say a word with regard to these plums and peaches. Everybody who lives in Ontario, especially in the southern portion, knows that we can grow those products there in superabundance. Not only can we grow enough to supply this Dominion, but to supply another dominion as well if we only had proper encouragement, but there are some things we need. We need better varieties. Those can be secured to a large extent by experimenting, and that can be done by the Mr. E. D. SMITH.
government a great deal more economically than by several thousands of different fruit growers. We have an experimental farm in British Columbia, two in the Northwest, one in Ottawa and one in Nova Scotia, covering a great variety of climate, but not one is so situated that those in charge of it can do anything in the way of experimenting with regard to the varieties of fruits grown in such quantities in the southern part of Ontario. Not one can grow fall wheat or Indian corn. We want an experimental farm in the southern fruit belt which will enable us to test the various kinds of fruits produced and do something in the way of hybridizing and creating new varieties, which will enable us to discover varieties, that will carry better than those we have at present. But even with the varieties we have we could supply the Northwest with all its requirements, if proper encouragement were given in the way of higher duty. Very large quantities of the fruits imported are a little earlier than our own, but there are very large quantities also which invade our markets when our own fruit can supply them. It may then be asked how is it that we do not do so ? One of the chief reasons is that our plums and peaches, being of a perishable nature, cannot, be set up on the shelves and sold like hardware or groceries or dry goods as the California plums and peaches can. These California fruits can be placed on the shelves and sold almost like turnips, and a good many of them do not taste very much better. Nevertheless they are handsome and have great keeping qualities, and the dealers prefer to handle them, no matter if their quality is not as good as ours, because they will keep longer and occasion no waste. The dealers can put them on the shelves and keep them there from day to clay until somebody comes along and buys them. They know exactly what profit they can get, just as in the case of dry goods and groceries, and have not to take into account any waste, whereas Ontario fruits require a good deal of skill in the handling and a good deal of energy and care. They must be put upon the market immediately, and the dealers must use energy and skill to have their customers take them off their hands quickly. That means trouble and annoyance, which the dealers in the Northwest do not like, and who can blame them ? That is the position in which our fruit growers are to-day. Then the dealers prefer to push these goods, on which they have no loss. They send their travellers all over the country. The wholesale fruit firms in Winnipeg are a very great power in that country, far different from the fruit dealers here. Here fruit is grown around every city, and a large portion of it is handled at retail upon our markets. But, in that great city of Winnipeg almost every pound has to be brought in, and the handling of that fruit is an enormous industry. So, the wholesale fruit merchants are a power. These fruit

merchants being able to handle this California fruit with so little loss are a powerful force against us. We want the government to come to our rescue and be a powerful force on our side. Surely it is to the interest of the government that this great industry that can be carried on so well in Ontario and in British Columbia should be made magnificently successful. For British Columbia is now coming forward as a fruit growing country. It is well known that in large districts in British Columbia fruit can be grown as perfectly as here, and in some places they grow fruit that will ship better than ours will. It is to the interest of the fruit growers of British Columbia and of Ontario to secure this market in the Northwest. Here, we have the great market of the Northwest, with a splendid fruit section on the coast to supply the western half of it, and another fine fruit section in Ontario to supply the eastern half. All we want is the assistance of the government to get a firm hold on that market. A few years ago, we had no hold upon it, no systematic effort being made on behalf of Ontario fruit-growers or on behalf of British Columbia fruitgrowers to assure Canadian fruit of a place in that market. In British Columbia the fruit-growers business has been, until very lately, in its infancy. You will read in the Winnipeg newspapers that the Ontario fruitgrowers are a lot of fools and do not know how to pack fruit. That is the method the wholesale dealers use to induce the people of the Northwest and Manitoba to believe that Ontario fruits are not the fruits to handle. I do not blame them. It is a matter of business with them, because they can make more money out of California fruit. But a great many people who come from Ontario, especially those now living in Manitoba, want our fruit. If it were not for the retail dealers who come from Ontario and the consumers there who know the fine, luscious quality of our goods, we would not get a little piece of that market, because, as I say we have the wholesale dealers against us. But, as long as we have the retail dealers and consumers on our side, we can capture a considerable portion of that market. We want to get into 'such a position that the Winnipeg merchants will find that they have to handle the Ontario fruit, and when they handle it they will find a way to get it into the hands of the consumer. Here, I say, is a way in which the govern-men can do something for the farmers of this country. They have not done it, but they ought to do it. If some hon. gentlemen opposite who speak in such laudatory terms of the government would spend the same energy in urging upon the leaders of the administration the importance of this method of doing something for the farmers, the fruit-growers and the market gardeners of Canada, they would be accomplishing more than by lauding the government to the
skies in the speeches they make in this House.
These are some of the ways in which the government can help the producers of this country. And I take it that the producers are the class who ought to be helped if any help is given out by the government. Almost everybody is a producer of something to sell ; farmers, manufacturers, miners and lumbermen are all producers, and these give employment to almost the whole population of our country. If the government looks well after the producers, I take it the consumers will be able to take care of themselves. A country in which the producers are making money is one that can afford to pay well persons engaged in professions, or others not producers. The producers of Canada can be assisted in different ways. I have mentioned one, and there is another, and a very important one. It is all very well for us to grow the best products, to manufacture the best goods ; but this will be of little use unless we can get these products and these goods to the market. It is true our home market is our greatest market, that it probably takes nine-tenths of our whole product. Nevertheless we have a surplus. As a great agricultural country, no doubt it will be a great many years before we shall be able to consume in the Dominion all the products of our farms. For many years to come we must have a large surplus to sell. And so, the government can do a great deal to assist us by perfecting the means of transporting our goods to the markets of the world, in the cheapest and most perfect fashion. We know that, in one respect we are situated more favourably than a.ny other country, while, in other respects our situation is not so favourable. We have the advantage of a great system of water transportation, including the magnificent river which carries our cargoes to the seaports. Even large ships can come far up into the interior of our country. But we know that our neighbours to the south, being energetic and determined that they will have, as they have had in times gone by, the major portion of the trade of carrying these goods, are continually improving their transportation facilities. It is the duty of our government to leave no stone unturned by which they can improve our transportation facilities and cheapen the carriage of our goods. I know they have undertaken a gigantic scheme to bring a portion of these western products to the sea-board. For my part I think that a large portion of that scheme will not tend to cheapen the cost of transportation. In no degree can it be shown that this extravagant scheme, calling for the expenditure of an enormous sum of money, and requiring the hauling of the goods for 1,800 or 1,900 miles through a country which is unproductive, can possibly be the cheapest means of carrying those", "goods out of the country. I think if even a small portion of this money were spent upon our great waterways and in the development of that system of transportation, far better results could be obtained than by the expenditure of this enormous amount on the scheme proposed by the government. We find that, in shipping grain from the upper lakes to Montreal, we have an advantage over New York of not less than li cents per bushel. But we find also that, when grain has to be transhipped at Montreal for Liverpool, we lose that 11 cents per bushel. The St. Lawrence route, though shorter than that by New York, is not developed. There are many hindrances, many obstacles, all of which I believe, could be removed by an energetic government. When we are compelled to pay at the port of Montreal so high a rate on goods brought down through our magnificent system of canals, which by the way was inaugurated and nearly completed under a Conservative administration -the advantage which' the country gains from its enterprise and great expenditure is neutralized. I find that last year we exported from the port of Montreal $70,000,000 worth of goods. For instance we exported 24,272,390 bushels of wheat, and on that we were compelled to pay 11 cents a bushel more than would have been paid for the carriage of wheat from Boston or New York. That amounts to $364,085. I. find that we exported from that port 21,182,840 pounds of butter and on that we paid 5 shillings a ton more than we would pay from Boston or New York. That amounted to $12,709.
We exported from Montreal 184,494,040 tons of cheese. We paid on that 3s. and 9d. a ton more than we would pay from Boston or New York. That amounted to $83,022.
Of apples we shipped 800,987 ban-els and paid 10 cents a barrel extra on them. This cost us $80,098. That makes a total of $539,914.
At the same ratio, if we took the balance of exports from Montreal and found the in crease-1 have no doubt that the freight rates were in the same proportion-we will find that the total excess freights amounted to $829,920. As the price we received for these export goods, to a large extent, sets the price of the goods sold in this country, there is no doubt that we lost a good deal more than this. It may be safely said that we lost $1,000,000 because the route from Montreal out past the banks of Newfoundland is not in the condition it ought to be in. First of all, the ships have to go slow a large part of the way, and cannot make good time. Then occasionally wrecks take place, and we have in consequence high insurance rates. The port of Montreal has large harbour dues, and ail these things combined with others that might he mentioned go to make up the reason why our steamers have to charge a higher rate of freight from that port notwithstanding that many of them are bonused. We pay out annually Mr. E. D. SMITH.
something between $100,000 and $150,000 to these steamers simply to come to Montreal. Ostensibly this is paid for the carrying of mail matter, but we only sent about thirty-nine tons of mail matter to the old country in the last year, ancl if you quadrupled the rates on ordinary freight the freight on this mail matter would toe only $1,500 ; yet we paid $150,000 to one line of steamers to go to Montreal and St. John, so that we ought to have the very best .service there. Some people say the insurance people have no right to charge the high rates that they do ; that they are discriminating unjustly against our routes. Whether that is so or not I cannot isay, but on looking at the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the past year X find that a considerable number of shipwrecks occurred on the St. Lawrence, and a large portion of those shipwrecks occurred through faults that might have been prevented if the Minister of Marine had in the last three years devoted his energies to thoroughly improving this St. Lawrence route, and if a proper pilotage system had prevailed, most of these shipwrecks could have been averted. Let me read the result of the examination by the commissioner, Mr. O. G. Y. Spain, into some of these ship wrecks,- and What he says in regard to the reasons why they occurred. I come first to the wreck of the steamer ' Oarrigan Head ' :
This British steamship grounded opposite No. 3 lightship, Lake St. Peter, River St. Lawrence, on April 24, 1903. A ,formal investigation was held into the casualty at the harbour commissioners' office, Montreal, and the finding of the court was as follows
That the captain was not to blame for the disaster. That the officer of the watch was not. to blame for the disaster. That the quartermaster carried out the orders of the pilot. That pilot Angers was not to blame. That the casualty was due to the buoys being out of place.
Why were the buoys out of place ? Why is there not a proper patrol over this river to see that the buoys are always in place 1 Surely it is the duty of the Minister of Marine and of the government to see that the buoys are in place. Had this been done the wreck would not have occurred, insurance rates would not be so high, and we would not have to pay such high freight rates on our produce.
Then there is the wreck of the steamship ' Iberian ' :
This British steamship grounded on the south side of the channel, near Isle aux Raisins, River St. Lawrence, on June 6, 1903, and at a formal investigation into the causes which led to the casualty, held at the harbour commissioners' office, Montreal, the court found :-
That nothing in the ship or her equipment contributed toward the accident.
That the conditions of the weather prevailing at the time of the casualty were favour-

That proper precautions were taken with regard to speed, the ship steaming about four (4) knots per hour", u'No wonder we have to pay high rates when ships can only go tour knots an hour. That is a fast Atlantic service. Surely that broad river, one of the most magnificent in the world, ought to be so improved, the channel of it ought to be so wide, so deep, so safe, that a steamer could go, not at i knots an hour, but at full speed night and day. The court is of the opinion, that the pilot, having proceeded about half the distance between the buoys without seeing the spar buoy he was looking for, should have anchored.
The next one is the steamship ' Protector ' :
This Norwegian steamship stranded at the mouth of the Saguenay river, on June 4, 1903, subsequently becoming a total loss. At a formal investigation into the case, held at the harbour commissioners' office, Quebec, the court found : -
That the ship was properly equipped and in a good and sea-worthy condition when she left Chicoutimi.
That she was supplied with proper and sufficient charts and sailing directions.
That the reef on -which she stranded was properly marked on the Admiralty charts.
That the entrance to the Saguenay rive'r is properly and sufficiently buoyed for the purposes of navigation.
That some blame attaches to the master for the stranding of the ship, in that he took no steps to ascertain whether the pilot was steering a proper course, in waters that any practical seaman could have navigated without the assistance of a pilot ; the channel being perfectly straight, and at no part less than six (6) cables wide.
That the master committed a grave error of judgment in taking no steps towards saving his vessel after stranding by jettisoning cargo from Nos. 1 and 2 holds and the deck cargo forward whereby the strain on the vessel would have been minimized, and the salvors enabled to place and work their pumps on arrival. The court is of the opinion that had
these steps been taken the vessel would have been" floated, and saved.
That the casualty was caused by the wrongful act of Pilot. Niazaire Delisle in steering an improper course, the evidence going to show that he had never piloted a vessel out of the Saguenay river before, and that ms knowledge of the river was so limited as to be dangerous.
Now, what I maintain is that no pilot should be retained on that river or allowed to navigate a vessel on the St. Lawrence unless he has a certificate that he is a practical experienced pilot of some standing. There is an opportunity for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to improve that route by establishing some more fog signals. The report of the commissioner appointed to investigate the wreck ot this vessel states :
That the aids to navigation-in so far as the fog-signal at Point des Monts iS concerned -were inefficient ; the evidence of various Witnesses going to show that it was impossible to hear the fog-signal, even after the vessel stranded, within a mile and a-half of the lighthouse.
These are the results of the examinations of a few of the wrecks that occurred, and they go to show plainly that the fault lies with the government and with the minister who is in charge of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It shows that he has not devoted his energies during all these long years to the improvement of this great rente, this route by which almost all the products originating west from the port of Montreal find their outlet to the sea. The evidence of these gentlemen appointed by tbe government themselves goes to prove that most of these accidents could have been prevented if proper signals and buoys had been provided. These are some of the things that I desire to call to the attention of the House, and I say that it is the duty of the government to bend their energies in this direction so as to make the St Lawrence route so safe that it will be as easy and as cheap to carry goods bv that route as by any other route1 from the Atlantic coast. There are other things that go to make that route cheap and safe. A large portion of the goods that we send from the port of Montreal are perishable goods. Three of our large exports are butter, cheese and apples. All of these are perishable products and require tbe best of care. It does not matter how much education our butter makers may have, it does not matter how much money may be spent upon educating our factory men to make the best butter that it is possible to make, it does not matter how much energy our farmers may bi mg to tbe work of producing good butter if you cannot carry it across the ocean m perfect condition. From $3,000,000 to $o.000,000 of our butter goes across the ocean and finds a market there. Most of it is sent m cold storage, and if we were to judge from the laudatory remarks which the lion, gentleman who last addressed the House made, we would come to the conclusion that the cold storage system as it at present exists is the most perfect in the world. We would imagine that every ship that sails from the port of Montreal is equipped with cold storage chambers that Mr. E. D. SMITH.
will carry every pound of butter across the Atlantic and land it in perfect condition in England where it will bring the highest prices. The cold storage system was inaugurated by the Hon. Mr. Montague when he was Minister of Agriculture, not at all, as the hon. member for West York tried to make this House believe, by the present hon. Minister of Agriculture. That system then inaugurated has no doubt become a great deal better than it was eight oi ten years ago. It would be a curious thing if after eight years of experience the Minister of Agriculture, with the able men lie has in bis employ, with the funds of the government at his disposal with which to equip these steamers as they are equipped except partially by the steamship companies, though the steamers sailing out of Boston and New York provide their own equipment, should not be able to carry out a better system of cold storage than that which previously prevailed. It would be dtrange if there was no improvement. There has been improvement. It would be strange indeed, after the long experience we have had with this very simple matter of cold storage, a thing that has been in operation in Australia and other portions of the world, which has been utilized for the carriage of perishable products to Great Britain for twenty years, a system which is in operation in all our cities and towns where you can place goods in cold storage and maintain them for months, if the government, with ample funds at their disposal, were not able to have a perfect system of cold stoiage. I am sure you will agree witb me that it is not very much to their credit that they have failed to perfect that system. Last year the hon. minister promised a thermograph record would be placed in every one of the chambers in ocean vessels for carrying perishable products. I find, however, that there are only 199 thermo-gi aph records taken, 155 in cold storage chambers, 32 in cooled chambers, and 12 in ordinary storage. Then I find the hon. minister in his report saying that a number of these boats carried butter in cold storage chambers at a temperature, not that which the hon. minister prescribes, but a temperature very far away from that which any experienced man knows they ought to maintain. The hon. minister maintained last year in his report 20 degrees as the proper temperature for the carriage of butter. Tbe butter shippers ask for a temperature of ten degrees. You would think that the boats would carry the butter below 32, the freezing point, but I find in the bon. minister's report that no less than nine boats carried it at an average temperature, not on a single day, but at an average temperature of over 32 degrees, and some of them averaged as higl^ as 40 degrees, 43 degrees, 36 degrees, 35 degrees, 39 degrees, 38 degrees, and so on.

I find on turning up the thermograph records that a very large number carried butter to London at temperatures ranging from below 32 degrees to 45 and 50 degrees. I find that the ' Iona,' sailing September 5, carried apples at a temperature of from 66 to 45 degrees. How could you expect apples, or pears, or any perishable fruits to be landed on the British market after a journey of fourteen days at a temperature of 45 degrees to 66 degrees, confined in a close cold storage chamber ? Then, I find that on the ' Hibernian,' sailing August 22, there was a temperature of from 68 to 42 degree ; on the ' Hurona,' sailing July 12, a temperature of from 50 to 40 degrees ; on the ' Devona,' June 28, a temperature of from 37 to 38 degrees, on the ' Iona,' June 13, a temperature of from 42 and 32 degrees, on the ' Kildona,' a temperature of from 42 and 29 degrees, during their respective voyages across the ocean. All these vessels carried butter at the temperatures which I have mentioned except the first two, which carried apples. Then, taking the Liverpool service, I find that the ' Ionian ' had a temperature of from 41 to 38 degrees, that the ' Kensington ' had a temperature of from 45 degrees to 30 degrees, and that a number of other steamers had temperatures very much higher than they ought to have been for butter. This goes to show that the cold storage system that the hon. member for West York lauded so highly is not the perfect success that the House might have been led to believe if they had accepted that hon. gentleman's remarks as representing accurately the facts of the case. I am not going to say there was not a very large number of boats which carried butter at a proper temperature. Certainly the large majority of them carried it at a proper temperature and there is a very great improvement in this respect, but the point I wish to make is : That after these long years of experience it is astonishing that there should have been a single cargo go out from the port of Montreal shipped in cold storage not carried at a proper temperature. Every one of these cargoes can be carried at a proper temperature. It is only a matter of looking after them properly. It is not that it can not be done, it is simply a matter that requires somebody to attend to it. There should be some body to keep urging it upon the steamship owners, who, I have no doubt would be quite willing if it were continually brought to their attention to see to it that a temperature was maintained to carry butter in a proper condition.
The result is that our exports of butter dropped from between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 worth to between $3,000,000 or $4,000,-, 000 worth. That is largely due to the fact that a great portion of our butter landed in England in a poor condition. Of course the blame was laid on the butter makers. My
experience is that if anything goes wrong the blame is put on the producer. He is a long distance off; he is not in parliament to defend himself ; he is not in the public eye, and so he is an easy mark for blame. Now, I doubt that the butter producer is responsible for this. I believe that the butter makers of Canada, with their experience) and intelligence, are able tq put up butter in as good shape as the people of any country in the world. I have no reason whatever to doubt that these cold storage chambers on the steamers with a temperature of 35 or 40 degrees instead of 20 degrees, are the sole and only cause why Canadian butter arrived in a mouldy condition on the English market, and why our exports of butter have decreased by millions of dollars. We were promised at the outset that this government would do a great deal for fruit-growers, and they started in a feeble manner to imitate the policy of Dr. Montague when Minister of Agriculture. Dr. Montague held that it was the duty of the government to see that Canadian fruit and butter were properly looked after in transit, and he could not understand why, if Australian fruit and butter could be carried through the tropics half way around the world in good condition, Canadian fruit and butter should not reach the English market in like manner. Dr. Montague experimented with butter. He bought a certain quantity of butter at 20 cents per pound, sold it in the English market, and proved that Canadian butter could compete with any butter in the world. Our butter export trade which was then practically nothing has since amounted to $5,000,000 and over some seasons. These experiments of Dr. Montague cost the country about $1,000, and I can well remember how the Liberals of that day loudly condemned the Conservative Minister of Agriculture for making this useless expenditure. But when they came to power, as they did in many other cases, they adopted the Conservative policy and swallowed themselves. They started experimental fruit shipments to the old country. They have been at it for eight years, and still without success. Let me point out that the Bartlett pear, one of our best pears, is a fruit that we ought to be able to ship in cold storage. I have kept them in cold storage in this country for several months, and I have taken them out in such sound and hard condition, that I have been obliged to put them in a warm rcom for a few days to ripen them sufficiently for use in the canning factory. Now, after eight years experimenting, the Minister of Agriculture is yet unable to have these Bartlett pears sent to England in good condition. We are voting here thousands and thousands of dollars to the minister and surely he should have sufficient control over his cold storage, to so regulate it that this", 'fruit might be carried for an ocean voyage of ten days and landed in sound condition on the English market. Yet, last year 1 believe there were only two carloads of these pears sent across, and both were an entire loss. In addition to apples, practically the only thing which the fruit-growers can ship in cold storage chambers at the present time, are some of our late fall pears that will keep in good condition in any old sort of place. Hr. Fisher and other gentlemen in the neighbourhood of Burlington have been shipping these pears for a number of years without cold storage, and have been making money out of the business. We can keep our pears in good condition in our own cold storage chambers and yet the Minister of Agriculture, to whom the member for West York gives so much credit and who has costly apparatus at his disposal, cannot arrange that they may be kept for the ocean voyage of ten days. But, Sir, only a comparatively small portion of our perishable goods require to go in cold storage. We export $20,000,000 worth of cheese, and that does not require cold storage. All that it needs is that the air should be constantly changed and kept as cool as the outside air of the ocean. The same thing applies to shipments of apples. On this side of the House I urged on the Minister of Agriculture years ago, that all that is required for cheese and apples was to have the steamer holds properly ventilated, I showed him the enormous loss that we were sustaining by the neglect of this precaution, but he did not heed us. It was at last ascertained, when we came to make a milder kind of cheese that it would not carry under the old conditions, and at last the commissioner appeared before the Agricultural Committee one day, and stated that our cheese had been so damaged during the previous year by being carried in ill ventilated steamship holds, that it had received a black eye in the old country, and he prophesied that for the following year our cheese exports would be reduced by $3,000,000. I thought that in all probability he was right, and I watched the matter closely, and true enough next year our exports of cheese instead of increasing by one and a half million dollars as had been usual, decreased by one million dollars, so that we lost about two and a half million dollars on our cheese exports for that year. I on this side of the House had cautioned the Minister of Agriculture year after year that this would happen; I told him the farmers of Ontario were losing at least a million dollars a year on their apple shipments on account of this fact, but the Minister of Agriculture did nothing. He only woke up when he heard from his commissioner. The minister sent a circular to the steamship owners asking them to Mr. E. D. SMITH.
provide that the holds should be ventilated.
The hon. minister thought to take a little credit to himself, and what did he do ? He came to this House and asked for a vote of $40,000-not to ventilate the steamers. That was a simple matter. He did not require any vote for that. All that was required was for him to point out to the steamship companies the necessity of the case, and to tell them that if they did not ventilate their holds, and let the agents of the government see that they were properly ventilated, he would report and publish the fact. That would not have cost the country a cent. But that did not suit the hon. gentleman. These hon. gentlemen opposite have come to regard money of so little account, that unless they can come to this House and ask for a vote of $100,000 or some other large amount, they do not think they can do anything for the people. So the hon. minister asked for $40,000, and that vote has been repeated several times, to assist the steamship companies to fit up their steamers with cool air chambers and a refrigerating plant and thus reduce the temperature below that of the ocean air. I had grave doubts at the time whether this would work out as the hon. minister seemed to think it would. I rather imagined that the steamship people, having to pay at any rate a portion of the cost of fitting up the steamers, and having to set apart a considerable amount of space for the refrigerating plant would have to charge a considerable extra rate for the use of them. The minister assured us that the rate would be the same. So the money was voted and the chambers were fitted up in a number of these steamers ; and what do we find ? We find that the temperatures in these cool air chambers are just about the same as in chambers which are properly ventilated. I find, for instance, that on the ' Cervona, ' the temperature of the cold air chamber was 62 to 54, and on the * ' Pretorian' with ordinary ventilated storage, 65 to 56 ; almost the same temperature. On the ' Kil-dona ' with cool air temperature 56 to 58 ; on the ' Ionian ' without cool air, the temperature was 45 to 62. I might read a dozen or so of reports of temperatures of steamers fitted up with cool air chambers : but I could only read twelve with regard to the ordinary storage, because these were all the hon. gentleman had recorded and it would be found that there is very little difference in this temperature in the cool air chamber and that in a properly ventilated chamber. It was pointed out to the minister last year that the only way to secure the object in view was to have his agents at Montreal, put a thermograph into every storage apartment, and have his agents on the other side examine them and report. This would not cost the country a single cent, as the bon. gentleman has his agents now. In order to see that the holds

are properly ventilated, he should have a compartment on deck or somewhere when the exact temperature of the ocean air would be recorded ; and if the record of that corresponded exactly with the record in the holds where the cargoes were, he would know that the fans were going; otherwise he would not know. It is all very well for him to have his agents go and see that the steamers are provided with the necessary apparatus ; but it is another thing to know that the apparatus is working all the way across the ocean. If it is not, it will not produce any result. In response to a question which I put to the minister last year, he promised that in every one of the holds carrying perishable cargo there would be a thermograph, but I find that they were only put into twelve ; but fortunately even these twelve show the advantage of them. I have examined the record of vessels going from Montreal on the same date and arriving on the other side at the same time. If the fans had been going and the holds had been ventilated, they would have shown exactly the same temperatures. I find that the ' Livonia ' had temperatures ranging from 45 to 60, and for five days the temperature was 50 or lower. I venture to say that in that case the fans were going and the ventilating apparatus was in operation. At the temperature which prevailed during those five days, you could carry summer apples, pears, or any other perishable cargo that goes from this country to the other side, except perhaps butter, and I do not know but you could carry that in a temperature of from 45 to 50, if you were sure of having it all the time. What do I find with regard to the 'Tritonia' that went at the same time ? She never showed less temperature than 60, and that only when loading, when the ' Livonia ' was about from 57 to 60. The * Tritonia ' showed a rise to 68 at about the same time as the ' Livonia ' showed from 45 to 50, and the temperature rose gradually until it reached 73, when the vessel was across to the other side ; whereas the ' Livonia ' never got above 55, a difference of from 15 to 18 degrees during the whole voyage. This is exactly the result which I wanted the minister to prove. There is the proof that it is absolutely necessary to take some steps to see that these steamers are ventilated. All you have to do is to put a thermograph, which costs $10, into each apartment which carries perishable goods and to put another on the deck. These thermographs will last a number of years, and by their use we could secure absolutely safe carriage for all our apples and cheese across the ocean. But that did not suit the hon. minister. He must put cool air apartments on the steamers at a cost of $100,000. and what has been the result ? That of 2,000,000 barrels of apples exported last year only 8,000 barrels were carried in cool air chambers, and that of 229,000,000 pounds of
cheese exported only about 3,000,000 pounds were carried in cool air chambers, that is, one cheese in seventy-five. Why was this 7 Because the shippers found that where the ordinary storage is well ventilated, they can carry cheese and apples across in as perfect condition as in the cool air chambers that cost the country $100,000 and in which shippers have to pay 36 cents a barrel extra on apples and ten shillings a ton extra on cheese. The shippers therefore will not ship in them, because they can get as good service without paying these extra charges. Since a large number of steamships have found it to be in their own interest to provide proper ventilation, these cool air chambers are neglected and the $100,000 is thrown away. This service, for which the people have to pay an enormously increased cost, is not required if the minister would do what he is asked to do by members on this side of the House. If the hon, member who preceded me had devoted a little more of his energies in this direction, he would have been of more value to his constituents. Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to detain the

House very long and I do not propose to weary it with long arrays of figures. The question of figures and statistics has been dealt with by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and by the hon. gentlemen who have spoken from this side of the House. I propose to deal more generally with the question. The right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) made a very charming speech. It gave great pleasure to the members on his own side of the House ; and we do not begrudge them that, because it is seldom they have had an occasion since this session open-end to indulge in a little fun or a little laughter. They had some justification for their mirth yesterday, because the figures with regard to our manufacturing industries quoted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce were amusing if they were not correct. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the statement of the Finance Minister, in which he was able to boast of continuous prosperity, must have been gall and wormwood to the members of the opposition. Let me tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce that he is mistaken there. No matter what party may be in power, the Conservatives of Canada will always be gratified when a Finance Minister in his budget speech is able to present indications that Canada is prosperous, even though mismanaged. The Minister of Trade and Commerce evidently cannot conceive that other men have loftier and more patriotic views than he entertains. The hon. gentleman inferentially took credit to the government that the farmers of Canada are more prosperous to-day than they were some years ago. Let me call his attention to the fact that in the states of the union which some years ago he so ably represented as immigrant agent, in Kansas, the Dakotas and thewestern states generelly, the farmers were in an infinitely more depressed condition than ever were the farmers in any part of Canada. During some years of prosperity the farmers in these states recovered their position, and so keenly did they rejoice at their translation from commercial slavery to freedom, that they made bonfires of the mortgages which they had redeemed and which at one time they thought must swamp them. Providence has sent to these states a bounteous harvest for several years in succession, and as the farmers of Canada have had the same experience of late years they are prosperous in a degree. The Minister of Finance presented a budget which was eminently satisfactory from several points of view. He was able to speak of large revenues, increasing deposits in the banks, progressive trade, and he took credit for that to the wise administration of himself and his colleagues. Well, Sir, the reason of this prosperity is that we have had good crops, higher prices for our produce, and greater areas of virgin soil brought under cultivation ; thus presenting to our people new
sources of wealth which we trust will be of advantage to our country for many years to come. The budget was more remarkable for what it omitted than for what it contained. The Minister of Finance presented a diagram, presumably to show the progress Canada has made since confederation ; but that diagram was remarkable for the omission of any indication as to the imports by Canada from the United States. It is a most extraordinary thing that the Minister of Finance shduld deliberately suppress the one part of that diagram which the government wished the country to be ignorant of. I do not think the Minister of Finance realized what he was doing when he deliberately placed before the country a diagram purporting to show the progress of every branch of our trade, and omitted to show our trade with our most important and largest customer, the United States. Another omission which is unprecedented is that the Minister of Finance made no reference whatever to the anticipated revenue and expenditure for the coming year. I presume we may take it for granted that there is an election to be held before next session, and that the Minister of Finance did not want to bring forward any estimate which might be found to be fallacious. There was another very extraordinary omission from the budget speech. This government has committed the country to an expenditure for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway of anywhere between $120,000,000 and .$170,000,000, adding 50 per cent to our national debt, and yet the Minister of Finance had not a word to say as to how this money would be raised or as to what effect the scheme will have on our future revenue and expenditure. These omissions were apparently made after great thought and deliberation. and evidently with the view of misleading the country. The election is near ; these figures would not be pleasant reading for government supporters in the political campaign, and so they are hidden from the people. The Minister of Finance claims that the debt of this country has not been increased during the eight years this government has been in power. That may lie true if we take as gospel the system of book-keeping which the Finance Minister has adopted, but even according to the minister's own figures he shows that this government has taken an increased taxation from the people of $57,800,000 as compared with the revenue under the Conservative government in like period, and yet the Liberal government has only reduced the debt by $1,084,000.	1 ' would point
out that the Minister of Finance takes credit on revenue account, for payments on account of public lands to the extent of $1,695,000, an item which surely should be credited to capital account, because we are using up the capital in our lands, and by no possible argument could this be credited on the revenue side of the

account. The erroneous and false method of book-keeping which the Minister of Finance has adopted, is an imitation of the vicious principle which has been followed by the Ontario government and I think by some other provincial governments.
They are crediting year by year to revenue account the money which they derive from sales of timber lands, amounting to enormous sums. They are making no provision to replace the capital which is exhausted from year *to year ; and as time goes on this, instead of being an asset, will turn into a liability. The exports from Canada to the United States in 1896 were $44 -448,000. in 1903 $71,783,000, an increase of $27,000,000. Our imports in 1896 were $58,570,000 and in 1903, $137,000,000. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, while not very sure about it, stated that it was probably a beneficial thing for the imports and exports of a country to be about an even keel ; which is the same as saying that a man who has $1,000 a year and spends the whole of it is about as well off as he would be if he spent only $750 and saved $250 for a rainy day. I find that the products of the forest exported from this country in 1903 amounted to $36,000,000. If we take the value of that timber in the stump, or the capital value belonging to this country, we find that we drew upon our capital last year to the extent of over $7,000,000. which went to swell the exports of the country and to diminish our assets. The expenditure in a growing country is naturally an increasing one', and I would not for a moment suggest that the expenditure to-day should be on the same plane as it was in 1896. But what I do claim is that the expenditure has gone up by leaps and bounds, that it is far in excess of the requirements of the country, and that it has not been caused by necessary works or proper development, but largely by extravagant expenditure and expenditure on useless works. All the work done by this government has been done at a cost vastly in excess of the cost under Conservative rule, while allowing for any increase in wages that may have occurred since 1896. I need only give one instance, that is the cost of taking the census. Any one comparing the cost of that service in 1901 and in 1891 will see at a glance that the extravagance there has been utterly reckless and uncalled for. The government have had at their disposal, without increasing the debt of the country, over $57,000,000. What have they done with it or what have they done for it ? They promised us before they came into power that they would give us a fast Atlantic service ; they promised vastly improved navigation on the St. Lawrence and on the great lakes. They have spent some money on the St. Lawrence, but the navigation has not been improved, as is evident from the increasing number of wrecks. On the great lakes I think I may safely say that nothing has been Mr. OSLER.
done since 1896 to render navigation safer. I do not know of half a dozen lighthouses erected since 1896 on the coasts of the great lakes, where the business is so enormous that we almost wonder where it comes from. If you take a marine map of the LTnited States coast, which also includes our coast, showing the lighthouse stations on the American coast, and then look at what we have, every Canadian should be ashamed of the negligence that has been displayed by Canada in this matter. I know that within the last three weeks vessels coming down and overtaken by fogs have been delayed for days on the coast because of the lack of foghorns and lights. It is claimed by the Finance Minister that the debt of this country lias not been increased, but that the debt per head has decreased. The debt per head in 1896 was $49.08 ; now it is $46.69, a reduction of $2.39 per head ; but the debt is spread over a larger number of people, which makes it smaller per head. The rate of taxation in 1S96 was $5.46 per head; now it is $8.87, or an increase of $3.41 per head, not on the old population on which the debt was figured, but on the increased population, showing the increased taxes per head to be more than the reduction of the debt per head for the whole eight years. Now there is no question that our trade is increasing. Our trade ought to increase. We have a vast area of virgin soil, we have enormous natural resources, and we only require to delve into these from year to year to increase our wealth, without reference to any government, good or bad. But a good government ought to so develop our natural resources and bring them before the people that wealth shall be obtained from them at the lowest possible cost and to the advantage of the greatest number of people. But I claim that the government have been absolutely neglectful of this vast natural wealth. ' Since 1896, when we were just beginning to realize what we had in this country, the government had taken over $57,000,000 out of the people, and what have they done to show to the people what our natural wealth is ? The only item in the whole list of expenditures that shows a decrease is the geological survey. I contend this government would have been wise, and and it would have had the support of every one on this side of the House, had it taken a sum going into the millions, to find out for the people of this country, in detail as far as possible, the extent of our natural resources, and the best way to utilize them. This government have not taken one single step towards that end. We have in this country great water-powers, vast timber resources, and immense deposits of minerals. We do not know any more about a great part of this country than we did two hundred years ago, as we found when the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill and its mountains of information were laid on this table. From Nipigon for hundreds of miles to the east we have only the reports of a few

surveyors and prospectors, who went up and down the rivers. We have no cross surveys and no adequate knowledge of the country. I contend that the first duty of the government, when it came into power, and knowing the strides which this country was making, was to have devoted a large sum of money each year to a systematic exploration of our country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, so that we should have at least some little preliminary knowledge of what we own. We would then have been able to deal intelligently with any scheme that was presented to this House.
People anxious to invest would be able to know where to go with the prospect of finding what they wanted, and we would be in a position to ascertain, to some extent at all events, the value of our national heritage. We are as ignorant of that to-day practically as we were thirty years ago. If England is anxious about her coal supply and is appointing commissions to inquire into the question, and if England put on an export duty on coal to prevent her natural resources in that commodity being depleted, is it not equally the duty of this government to try and arrive at some idea of our natural resources ? We are depleting our timber at a rate which no one in Canada realizes. It is quite true that this timber is more or less under the control of the different provinces, but surely it is in the interests of the country at large that this government should suggest the taking of some steps in order to reach an agreement among the provinces on some plan for the reforestering of the immense tracts which are now being laid bare. The greatest wealth Canada possesses is being exhausted and without our getting practically any return compared with the enormous value we are losing. Although this matter comes not directly under the control of this parliament, surely it is something concerning which this parliament 1 might well take steps to initiate some policy or have some policy adopted by the provinces. If England is anxious about her coal, is it not time that we should be anxious about our timber ? In the United States their timber wealth has been enormously reduced, and the different States of the Union are beginning to realize that the greatest mistake they ever made was in not replanting the forests which were cut down. In the old world one of the most important branches of every government is the preservation of its timber resources, and the cutting of timber is there regarded as almost a sacred thing. That will be the case some day in this country, but the longer you put off dealing with the question, the greater will be our loss.
Suppose we undertook to reforest the province of Ontario, would not the timber become the property of that province, and we won 1 d incur all the expense ?

I am sure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) is not serious. Now, there is one principle which, I think, is accepted by political economists without exception ; and that is, that if there is to be a tariff, that tariff should be as simple as it is pos-

sible to make it; it should be so plain that there need be no difficulty in interpreting it, and so simple that it may be brought into effect with as little friction as possible and as little difficulty to both importer and seller. But this extraordinary, bungling tariff that the Minister of Finance has submitted is so complicated that, I will be bound to say, it will have to be changed before the next session. It is almost impossible to define any articles under that tariff. Some importer, let us say, calls the attention of the government to the fact that a certain article is being brought in at a slaughter price. The government have to find out what the market price of that article really is. It may be an article the price of which may suddenly and greatly change, as for instance rails or some other iron product, the fall in the price of which according to our experience may be from twenty to forty per cent within three weeks. In such a case the government will be absolutely unable to deal with the question in such a fashion as to do justice to the parties. This change puts in the hands of the government an arbitrary power, it even puts in the hands of the officials of the government an arbitrary power, to help their friends and put obstacles in the way of men rvho do not agree with them, this difficulty being a clear, gratuitous addition to the ordinary difficulties there are in every case in the carrying out of the details of a tariff policy. The government have, we contend, increased the expenditure of this country without giving value for the money which they have taken out of the pockets of the people. They have not spent money in developing the country in the manner which they promised and which the country would support. They have not taken as efficient steps as they should have taken to ascertain the value of our natural heritage, and they are allowing that heritage to go' to waste because of the lack of information. The government have not given adequate protection, they have not given the protection which is due to the men who have put their money into manufacturing enterprises in this country. They are dealing with these industries from time to time as it may suit them, or as the necessity of the case may be forced upon them, and in that way they are destroying the confidence of the people in the stability of our tariff and the safety of investing money in our enterprises. Two years ago, I think it was, they proposed an enormous bounty on our steel, which' would affect principally the works in Nova Scotia. In addition to
this the government say that bounties are a capital expenditure.
I do not intend to occupy the time of the House longer, but I wish to say a word to show the difference between the two parties. The policy of the government is one of vacillation, of taking advantage of the condition of affairs from day to day, of advocating one policy in one place and at one time and another policy at another place and another time, as it may suit the people whom they address. They have not realized that in this country the first necessity is to have a fixed policy so that every man *who runs may read, and every man who goes into business may know that he is protected and that he is entering that business under certain conditions. Another difference between the two parties is that the Conservative party have always believed in the future of their country. The gentlemen who are now in pow7er. more especially the men who spoke so eloquently and so enthusiastically yesterday, never believed in their country in times of depression, and did all in their power to belittle this country and to destroy its credit, by writing letters to the ' Economist,' to the public press, by advising our men to leave this country-they did all In their power when this country was undergoing a period of depression to belittle It and, in a measure, to throw dirt on it. The Conservatives today are as delighted, as proud of the prosperity of this country as any member on the other side of the House, and I say further that if it should be the misfortune of this country to again drift into a period of depression, no man on this side of the House will be found throwing dirt at the country or decrying its future. The Conservative party have always had, have to-day and will always have, confidence in the country, whether in prosperity or in adversity.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) argued that inasmuch as we exported from_this country last year lumber which, upon the stump, would have been worth seven millions of dollars, we had thereby, so to speak, exhausted the capital or the assets of this country to that extent. I noticed that, later on, the same gentleman thought that we had not expended sufficient sums in geological surveys of this country for the purpose, I suppose, of ascertaining its mineral and other resources, in order that these might be exploited. Does not the hon. gentleman see that so long as these minerals remain in the land and are not shipped out of Canada, we are not exhausting the assets of Canada ? Does the hon. gentleman not see the danger of his argument in calling for the exploitation of

these natural riches ? If we are losing Canadian wealth in sending our fine timber out of the country, then in like measure we are exhausting her wealth by shipping minerals out of the country. Sir, this is simply to reduce that argument to an absurdity. The fact is, that if we export that timber from this country and get back money return for it, either money or something equally valuable in kind, that money increases the capital of this country, and we are thereby enabled to develop those same mineral resources about which the hon. gentleman has so much anxiety. Then what about the growth of our forests V I have been told that there are already in existence in Canada limits on which the lumbermen are now beginning their second cut after thirty years' of cutting upon them. Some gentleman says it is an edition de luxe; I hope I have suggested a reductio ad absurdum. I would pass away from this subject interesting though it may be, and I come to the budget speech so ably presented by the Minister of Finance. I may say that so far as the county of Haldimand is concerned, an agricultural county in the main, 1 believe that the' changes in the tariff announced by the Finance Minister will he eminently satisfactory. 1 know that the reduction of the duty on coal oil will be a satisfaction to the people there, because they have been asking for it for years past. I was somewhat surprised to find that the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) is opposed to the reduction of the coal oil duties, but then lie lives in a city where they illuminate their houses with electric light and gas, and he has little sympathy -for those of us in the country who have to depend on tallow dips or coal oil. The prohibition of the importation of inferior animals will be welcomed by the farmers of this country, because if there is one thing which the Canadian farmer wishes more than another it is improvement in our herds, and the announcement of the Finance Minister in this respect tells of a movement in that direction. The free importation of animals to improve breeding,-even including the goats about which certain unsympathetic remarks have been made-is also a move in the right direction, as is also the free importation of ferment cultures for butter making.
But, Sir, while my county is au agricultural county in a large measure, it has started on the road of being a manufacturing county as well. We have at Niagara Falls an immense power development going on ; we expect when that is completed that many thousands of horse-power will he distributed ail over the Niagara Peninsula and we hope to get the advantage of cheap power. When that power is distributed among our small towns the people of Haldimand expect a growth in their manufacturing industries. And so, Sir, we view with great satisfaction the announcement of the government that it has said ' stop,' to that dumping process to which no patriotic Canadian can for a moment consent. We are not in my county free traders to a degree, nor protectionists to a degree. We believe in building up Canada ; we believe there should be fair competition. I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that so great is the manliness of the people in my section of the country that they do not fear fair competition, but when that competition

Is not fair, when it becomes assassination in place of trade, then the people I represent will stand for the government which is the first government in the history of the world to have framed legislation to stop that abuse which has crushed out so many infant industries in various other countries. That announcement of the Finance Minister will be received with eminent satisfaction in the part of the country which I represent.
And now taking up more particularly what I intended to deal with, I need not apologize to the House for so doing. That pamphlet No. 15 on the face of it is so absolutely silly, is so absolutely dishonest, that we Liberals, from the party standpoint would rejoice to see it find its way into every house in Canada because we can disprove its statements from end to end, and in doing so we can shake any of the little confidence still re-nahining in the people of Canada in that Conservative party which once was great. I go on then to two items which alone more than account for the increased expenditure. So we call in the old paper and issue new paper. We are not going to apologize for that ; and that accounts for over $54,000 of the increase. The balance is due to the increased charges we have paid in London for bill stamps. As you know, we, | in concert with most other colonies of

Great Britain, go to the London money market for our financial requirements, and are governed by the conditions there obtaining.
