There is the $618,277.10 accounted for, then, in less than sixty seconds by the clock.
In premium discount and exchange, we spent less by $51,064.69 than hon. gentlemen opposite. But I want to be perfectly fair and frank in the discussion of this subject, claiming credit for the government only when it is their due, and blaming the Conservatives only when they are deserving of blame. This matter also is controlled by conditions in the money market of Great Britain, over which we have no control, and for which no government, whether Liberal or Conservative, can properly be blamed or praised.
I therefore pass on to the next item, civil government, in which I find an increase of $132,563.75. This is but an increase of 9 per cent in eight years, a little over 1 per cent per year, a very small increase in this item in view of the vast increase in the commerce of the country and in its population, bringings as it always does increased business in the government offices. The public accounts give thirty-three subheadings under this caption, and almost every one of these could be subdivided.
I would not be justified in taking up the time of the House in so minute an analysis ; but if hon. gentlemen will take the time to make it, they will find that the minutest item of expenditure is as justifiable as the largest which I have quoted. Yet I would have you note this fact, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservatives in tlleir term of office, during Canada's sluggish time, as I may fairly call it, increased the expenditure under civil government by no less than $35,000 a year, while we, in these growing times, have only increased it by $20,000 a year.
To the expenditure for administration of justice the same remarks would very well apply. There is an increase of $204,265.11, but of that $120,400.41 is on account of the Yukon, and the Yukon, as I propose to prove, has paid for the Yukon. We can, therefore deduct that amount. This leaves but $83,865.70 of an increase, and when we think of the increased business before the

courts, that seems a very narrow amount t>y which to have augmented the cost of the administration of justice in this country. 1 will call attention to a further thing. Hon. gentleman after hon. gentleman opposite has risen in this House and recommended that the salaries of the judges in Canada should be materially increased. I must say that in that I think hon. gentlemen opposite are right, for occasionally even they are right. That is not the point under discussion, however. The point is that had the government acceded to their request, this increase in the administration of justice would have been still more largely augmented. That being the case, it does not lie in the mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite to say that we had already increased it too much.
The expenditure under Dominion police has increased by $6,337.21 an increase so small that X would not weary the House with it, but for my desire to be accurate and complete in the statement I am making. We have increased the number of men somewhat. and we have increased their pay somewhat because of changed conditions and the increased amount of work they have to do. I may say that, under the very able command of Lieut.-Colonel Sherwood, of Ottawa, that force has reached a state of efliciency unexcelled on this continent. We have no apologies to make for the Dominion police. Passing on to legislation, I find an actual decrease in the expenditure of SI52,365.72. This is a decrease for which unlike the decrease which I noted under ' premium, discount and exchange, ' we can really claim some credit. How does it come that we have managed so materially to lower the expenditure on legislation ? Xet me give you one item, Sir, which far more than accounts for it. We have abolished, as we promised, that heavy burden, the Franchise Act. In 1895 that Act cost us $239,963.33. But in 1903, because we sent it into the abomination of the scrap heap, the cost is not one cent. Thus by doing away with that cumberous and expensive machinery no less a sum than $239,963.33 was saved at one stroke. If I may be allowed a parenthesis for one moment, I may say that we take credit, not only for having saved that amount of money, but for having abolished something which was almost intolerable. Any hon. gentleman who has worked in the province of Ontario in connection with the voters' lists, under the old Act, knows the difference between then and now. In the old Act there was an income clause requiring that a young Canadian, if not a property owner or a farmer's son. must be in receipt of $150 per annum before he could exercise the privilege of citizenship ; and often did I argue that a youth who was getting $12 per month and washing and mending was entitled to vote, because $12 a month represented $144 a year and surely the washing and mending
represented the other six. But since the Liberals have come into power, the right of a young man to exercise the franchise no longer depends on the value of sewing on his shirt buttons and mending his socks. The days of small things are over. Perhaps my hon. friends opposite will say that they are over in expenditure also. Well, I hope they are, provided the expenditure is a wise and prudent expenditure. I come now to the subject of penitentiaries, which I am sure cannot seriously interest any member of this House. In 1895 our expenditure was $449,599.81 and in 1903 it was $477,839.82, showing a gross increase of $28,241, but we have also increased our revenue by $15,012.56, leaving a net increase of only $13,277.45. That increase is more than accounted for by the purchase of a quarry at Kingston, by putting in brick making plant at St. Vincent de Paul, by increasing the salaries of the wardens and keepers, and by the increased cost of supplies for the maintenance of these institutions. So that the smallness of the increase is an evidence of economy and not of extravagance. In arts and agricultural statistics, there is a large increase of no less than $326,271.73, the expenditure having been in 1895, $216,740.30 and in 1903 $543,012.03. But of this increase $100,000 is due to the increased cost of the census as compared with what hon. gentlemen opposite paid in 1895. I shall not discuss that subject, because it was most ably dealt with by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He put the case in a nutshell, and we say that the reason w,e have paid so much more for our census than our hon. friends opposite did for theirs, is the good, valid and proper one that broadcloth always costs more than shoddy. The next item of increase is that of $59,540.27 on exhibitions. But who will say that these exhibitions, in which we have so prominently and creditably figured for the last few years, have not had a very large share in inducing the great increase of immigration to Canada on which we are to-day congratulating ourselves ? At one time Canada appeared before the eyes of the world as a place of ice and snow, only fit for the habitation of esquimo, but when the people of Paris saw the magnificent crops of peaches and fruits of all varieties that are grown in this country, they naturally said to themselves :	these do not grow in snowbanks. This expenditure therefore has been a very wise one, and is one of the causes of the increased influx of people into this country. We come then to agriculture and dairying, and in this item there is an increase of $177,092.50 over 1895. If I were to go into the details at length, that would lead me into a particular discussion of the question of cold storage. I shall not weary the House by going into that question, because we have dealt with it before and it may come up again in some other shape, but shall confine myself to this point of that

subject. Our bon. friends opposite claim that they inaugurated cold storage. So they did, but it was cold storage of so inefficient a character that Australian butter, which had a much longer distance to go, was bringing at that time from ten to twelve shillings per hundred pounds more than Canadian butter in the British market. But after the present government had perfected the system, the conditions became changed and almost the reverse was the case, which goes to prove that whereas Australia had a perfect system of cold storage, hon. gentlemen opposite had a poor one, not because a good system could not be got, but because they did not know how to get it. 1 pass on to immigration, a subject which has been largely dealt with by previous speakers. The amount of the increased expenditure on immigration is $447,860.77, but I would call attention to the fact that whereas in 1895 we had had but 2,394 homestead entries, in 1903 we had 31,383, and whereas in 1895 we had but 18,790 immigrants, in 1903 we had 128.364. And, of these 128,000, 91,265 were English speaking, the kind we value more than almost any other, except perhaps some from the northern states of Europe. And X would further call attention to this point, that last year these people cost Canada but $5.02 per head, which is a decrease of $2.32 per head compared with the preceding year. This goes to show that Canada is becoming so well known and advertised, through our expenditure that people are flocking to it in increased numbers at a decreased expenditure per head and that the seed generously sown is now giving an equally generous return. Think of 9,387,561 acres of land being acquired by settlers through purchase and free homesteads, or as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, remarked, more than half the lands of Ontario under plough now in one single year. Think what that is going to mean. In 1895 there were sold but 114,713 acres for $222,489. whereas last year there were 4,229,011 acres sold for $14,651,757. The increase is not only in acreage, but also in the price of the land sold. It represents an advance of fifty per cent in the value of the land per acre in those eight years of Liberal rule. So we might continue ad nauseam, though I fancy a good patriotic Canadian could take a pretty good deal of this splendid progress without feeling sick over it. But time presses. The next item is that of quarantine which shows an increase of $162,010.61. I do not wonder that Conservatives did not spend more than they did in 1895, because our quarantine is composed of two sections-the human quarantine and the quarantine of animals. They had only 18,000 people to look after,-so far as quarantine of immigrants went-whereas we had 128,000. Therefore they did not require to spend so much on human quarantine. That accounts for $70,000 of this increase, and the balance is due to the extreme care and watch-Mr. A. T. THOMPSON.
fulness of the department in keeping disease out of the flocks and herds of Canada. Previous to the advent of the Liberals to office, there was an embargo placed by the United States on Canadian cattle, but the hon. Minister of Agriculture succeeded a few months after he took office, in having that embargo removed.
You will remember, Sir, the immense advantage that was to the people of Canada ; how our exports went up from 4,000 cattle in four and a half years bringing us $50,000 to a number bringing us in hundreds of thousands of dollars to say nothing of the increase in value of cattle on the local market. Our cattle now, I admit, are largely going to the Northwest ; but, even last year, we shipped 10,000 cattle to the United States. That in itself is a considerable item which the farmers in Canada would not like to lose. If we prevent the spread of contagious diseases among our cattle we" keep open the United States market. But, so soon as these diseases become prevalent in Canada the Americans will put on the embargo and we shall And ourselves with the market of the United States shut against us as well as the market of Great Britain which has been closed to us so long and which we have made such efforts to reopen.
In pensions the increase is only $3,575.39. But this is almost a purely automatic increase.
I pass now to superannuation, where there is an increase of $81,033.21. I fancy I hear some gentlemen of the opposition saying, during the general elections which may possibly be upon us in a year's time or less : An increase in superannuation ? We understood you Liberals were going to abolish superannuation. Sir, so far as the future is concerned, we have abolished it But we are reformers, not despoilers. We have no desire to interfere with those civil servants who came in under the old (Superannuation Act. influenced, largely, no doubt in seeking employment in the civil service by the knowledge that their declining years would be taken care of. So, we pay to these people the superannuation guaranteed to them when they entered the civil service. But, we have passed an Act abolishing superannuation since July 1, 1898, so far as regards all those who entered the civil service after that date. So, this increase of $81,033.21 is not our increase, but represents what we are bound to pay because of the contracts of hon. gentlemen opposite. Therefore, we wipe this off the account.
Then, militia calls for an increase of $388,995.62. Of this, $270,231.89 is under the head of pay of staff, permanent force, active militia, allowances, clothing and necessaries. It is a well known fact that this increase was not because of an increase of pay to the men. Many of us thought that the pay to the men should be increased. But the government could not see eye to eye with us

until this session, and so kept the pay at fifty cents per day for the private soldier. What has this increase been expended on ?
I will tell you. For one thing, on the purchase of clothing, equipment and so on. So, while we have spent a larger sum our wardrobe is now fairly well supplied, whereas, in the days of Conservative rule it was meagre in the extreme ; and how we could have fitted out our regiments in case of necessity arising to increase them to a war strength, or anything like it, passes my comprehension. That is an expenditure for which we have the goods in store to show, something that hon. gentlemen opposite will not cavil at. And this accounts for $270,231.89 of this increase.
The coronation contingent cost $02,630.43.
I must assure you, Sir, that the coronation contingent gave excellent value for the money it cost. The British papers were full of favourable comments. We think that that contingent did not disgrace the country that sent it forth ; and we believe that had hon. gentlemen opposite been in power-for we think their loyalty almost equal to our own-they would have despatched such a contingent under similar circumstances.
The Dominion arsenal cost $96,403.99 more. But, then, we are able to turn out three times as many cartridges as we could under hon. gentlemen opposite. And that is an absolute necessity in view of the spread of rifle clubs which require ammunition for their practice. If there is one thing on which hon. members of this House seem to be a unit, it is on the advisability of the organization of these rifle clubs. But you can understand, Mr. Speaker, that a rifle club without cartridges, to shoot would not be good for much. They would be much in the position of a rifleman of whom the story is sometimes told. He aimed at the target several times and failed to hit it : and was told by his commanding officer to fix bayonets and charge it. That would be about the position of rifle clubs without cartridges-they might become proficient in the use of the bayonet but they would never learn to shoot.
In Mounted Police the increase was $343,909.75. Well, why should there not be an increase 7 Look at the number of people going into the west. Would it be surprising | if an increase in expenditure on mounted police were found necessary ? But you will be surprised to learn, Sir,-no, I beg your pardon, you will not be surprised to learn, Mr. Speaker, because you keep yourself well nosted on the questions of the day ; but hon. gentlemen opposite will be surprised to learn-that this increased expenditure on mounted police is not because of the development of western Canada, but it is because of the number of police we have had to send to keep order in the distant district of the Yukon. We find that, as against this increase of $343,909.75 for mounted police no less than $590,702.93, or 144
almost twice the sum is chargeable to the Yukon. And the Yukon has paid for the Yukon. Therefore, instead of having spent more money on the mounted police, there has been a decrease, service for service, as compared with the expenditure of hon. gentlemen opposite, in spite of the great increase in population in the Northwest. That is, because of the better administrative ability shown by the Minister of the Interior, we have actually been able to reduce the expenditure on this service.
On public works chargeable to income the increase is $2,323,236.38-a very large increase, I grant you. But what are the facts? Our total expenditure was only $4,065,553.27 -in this young and lusty and growing country of Canada, requiring the development and improvement of the public works over an enormous area ; half a continent, no less. Why, in 1896, our Conservative friends were prepared to spend-including their main and supplementary estimates the latter of which were printed but not brought down-$3,998,010, or actually, within $60,943 of what we spent this last year. And their income then was $34,000,000 and their expenditure $38,0ou,000, a deficit of $4,000,000, whereas our income is $66,037,068.93 for the year, with a surplus of $14,345,106.17- a very different state of things indeed. But there is, I think, still another reason why this increase is beyond cavil. We Liberals will not object to it, this expenditure of the government to whose support we of the back benches are pledged to the very last man, a government that we honour and venerate, a government that, behind its own closed doors is a happy family. We will not cavil at the increase. And how can hon. gentlemen cavil at it in'View of the fact that it is less by $155,740, than the expenditure of the year before, made under the then Minister of Public Works, the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Mr. Tarte) who has since been welcomed to the organization of the Conservative party-welcomed back I must say-the man whom they discovered, they tell us, to have been the custodian of the brains of the Liberal cabinet. His expenditure was no less than $155,740 greater, and he is now declared by our friends opposite to be a great administrator and an able financial genius.
Next, we come to railways and canals. We find there an increase iu the expenditure chargeable to consolidated fund of $75,599.52. Well, we have somewhat increased the mileage of our railways and canals. And, as you increase public works, it necessarily follows that the expenditure upon them must increase, for the greater the quantity you have to look after the higher the expenditure for up-keep must be.
Then, you have mail subsidies and steamship subventions, an increase of $286,017.96. Do not hon. gentlemen opposite know that the increase of our commerce is owing largely to the fact that we ourselves have taken



means to open up new channels of trade. We believe that that is the way to increase trade and we are confident that the people of Canada believe it also. We have no fewer to-day than thirty-three services, as against eighteen in 1S95, under bon. gentlemen opposite. The principal new ones are those to Prance, to Belgium, and to South Africa. And we hope that very shortly indeed a new service will be inaugurated between this country and the great republic of Mexico, with its population twice as great as ours-this service being the result of the so-called junketing tour of that energetic and able gentleman the Postmaster General and Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock).
That junketing tour, Sir, which he took actually at his own expense, if we except possibly the cost of the axle grease on the government car which otherwise would have been rusting on some siding in Canada. He went at his own expense throughout, and, with his eyes open, as always, to the advantage of Canada, he studied existing conditions and we hope and believe that the result will be that he will establish still another steamship service, both on the Atlantic and the Pacific, which will still more largely increase the foreign trade of Canada. I shall refer to some more of the delightful Tory campaign literature. I ask hon. gentlemen if they are proud of leaflet No. 13, which speaks of a minister of the Crown, going on a junketing tour to see the gaisha girls of Japan. It may be a funny thing, it may excite a smile, but is it quite worthy of the party which has rejoiced to call itself the gentlemen's party. I am glad to see that the man who wrote that article has been overruled by his friends in the party and that in the larger page subsequently published that disgraceful reference-for it is nothing else-is omitted and while his trip is mentioned, there is no nasty, low insinuation coupled therewith.
So we pass on to ocean and river service, in which there is an increase of $212,043.91. This expenditure is in the interests of commerce and of this amount we are expending on Dominion steamers, $100,000 more than the Conservatives spent, and for this last year we paid nearly $100,000 as a balance for a steamer to replace the ' Newfield.' The Conservatives had no similar item in 1895. These two items practically account for the increase.
Then we come to lighthouse and coast service. This is almost an incredible case. There is an increase of $488,240.42. Our Conservative friends spent in 1895, $12,219,29 on lighthouses, and we are spending* including a steel lightship for the Lurcher shoals, $397,375.85, almost $400,000. And yet the junior member for West Toronto, (Mr. Osier) was good enough to say that we are neglecting the improvement of navigat-Mr. A. T. THOMPSON.
ion on our waterways, notwithstanding the fact that we are spending $400,000 to their $12,000 in the improvement of our lighthouses/ in Canada. To my mind that fact speaks for itself. The only excuse that can be made for the Conservatives for neglecting the lighthouses is that they had very little commerce to light in the days when they controlled the destinies of this country.
I now pass on to still another heading, to wit, marine hospitals. In that there is an increase of only $10,161.10. I believe that an extra wing was built which accounts for part of this increase, but apart from that I can dispose of this increase quickly and satisfactorily in this manner :	more commerce, more sailors, more sailors, more sick. Surely that is a precise way of dealing with the subject. I suppose that our merchant marine has enormously increased,' and it is reasonable to suppose that with that increase the number of sailors will also increase.
I come now to steamboat inspection in which there was an increase of only $3,786.21. This is a still smaller item wTith which I would not deal at all except for the sake of accuracy, and I might again say : more imports, more steamboats ; more steamboats, more inspection. The revenue from this source has so increased that it almost balances the increased expenditure.
In the item of insurance inspection, there is an increase of $4,929.75, a small item mentioned also for accuracy. Of this amount $3,691.63, nearly the whole amount, came back to us in increased fees.
Then we come to fisheries, in w'hich there was an increase of $84,006.17. Will any lion, member on the opposite side from the maritime provinces-and there are still some remaining, although. Mr. Speaker, if we can read aright the signs of the times, there will shortly be few maritime members on your left-will any of that remnant say to me that this government has spent too much on the fisheries of Canada ? When we remember that of this amount some $37,610 was spent in fish breeding and that $11,331.49 of the small increase was spent for supplying cold storage for bait of deep-sea fishermen, the increase seems very slight. On this service we spent $527,829.12 against a Conservative expenditure of $443.822.95.
On geographical surveys there was an increase of $10,594.85. On this subject the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) himself answered the complaint. We spent but $78,746.26. That hon. gentleman says we should spend millions on it. That show's the consistency of hon. gentlemen opposite. They make wholesale charges of extravagance, and wrhen we come to the items their cry is that we do not spend enough, that we should spend more. I have yet to find an example where hon. gentlemen are not

Inclined to go one better and yet they make that general omnibus charge of extravagance against us.
On scientific institutions there was an increase of $-49,512.63. That surely is money well spent. What increases the riches of a country so much as the advancement of science ? What is going to overcome that sad lack under which the provinces of Ontario and Quebec so long laboured, the absence of coal ? The advance of science, the advance of knowledge of electricity by which, taking advantage of our enormous water-powers, we will be able to smelt ores by water-power, through one transforming stage, that of electricity. We know how this enterprising government sent men to the old country to study the question of smelting ores by electricity, and we know also that, smart and clever and businesslike as are our American brethren to the south of us, great as are their resources and enterprise, they never sent a commission abroad to find out this for themselves. 1 hope that as a result of that knowledge which we have obtained by this means, before a great while we will have immense and valuable enterprises in portions of Ontario and Quebec where in the past such development was utterly impossible owing to the fact that we had no coal for smelting.
In subsidies to provinces there was increase of $151,828,42. Why not ? Is that not fixed by statute ? Is that not a matter of population of provinces ? I would not object if it was $1,151,000, because an increase of that amount would mean that our population had grown by leaps and bounds. No apology need be made for such an increase, nor yet for the increase in the item for the poor Indians.
Under the heading of Indians there is an increase of $122,411.24. Time was when possibly politicians might have spent a little more than was . equitably due upon the Indians. That was in the days of hon. gentlemen opposite, when they gave these wards of the government the right to vote. In my part of the country, in Haldimand, and the adjoining constituency of Brant, we have Indian reserves and I am bound to say that when I think over the record of these poor Indians, I am almost inclined to think that perhaps it was cruel to deprive them of the franchise for I know that they were more active voters than white men are. In the famous Coulter and Montague election, I remember that on one of the Indian reserves, before 8.30 in the morning-I will admit with the aid of certain white necromancers and scorcerers-14 dead Indians voted. But who will say that to-day any government will spend too much money upon the Indians since we know they are now devoid of political influence ? The fact is that this government has adopted the very wise policy of educating the Indians so that they may become estimable and valuable 144 i
citizens. We spend a large amount of money to bring people from the old world to the new. Is it not reasonable and decent to spend upon the aboriginal inhabitants of this country, the men who owned it before the foot of white man ever trod its shores, a reasonable amount of money to bring them up to a condition of something like equality with ourselves ?
Then I pass to the government of the Northwest Territories. There was an increase there of $498,839.72. I shall not discuss that for one moment. We know the increased number of people who have gone in. We know the vast amount there is to do in these territories and no man will say that we have spent too much money there. We have to make these incoming settlers comfortable, we have to give them safe and stable government there. Did we not do so, they would write back to their friends, the influx of population would cease and those who had already gone into the country would, as in the days of Conservative rule, leave the country and establish their habitations to the south of the boundary line. We come now to miscellaneous. There is an increase here of $311,396.32. It divides itself into a great number of subheadings. 1 hardly think I dare venture to take up the time of the House in discussing these subheadings.
Go on.

I shall only mention a few of them. First, there is the Paris agency, $6,500,- a new service entirely. You cannot make an omelet without breaking some eggs. Look at the magnificent trade omelet we have made for this country. One of the eggs that we have broken to get this trade omelet is the Paris agency, which has cost us $6,500, a mere bagatelle compared with the increased commerce we will get from that source in the future. The next is the astronomical observatory and apparatus, $10,497.85. That is a service in the interest of science. The next is the result of the increase in the gold output consequent upon the discovery of gold in the Yukon, being the assay office, tlie increase being $14,993.90.
Hon. gentlemen opposite did not require anything of the sort ; in fact, I do not know that in those days there was really enough gold in Canada to require an assay to be made of it. Then, we return to Messers. Petersen, Tait & Company, the amount of their deposit, $56,940. That was money which they had paid into the treasury. They got it back out of the treasury and there was no loss in the transaction. The next is half-breed claims commission, $2,978.24. Why do I mention such a small sum as this ? Just to emphasize the business-like methods of this government in contradistinction to the unbusiness-like methods of the late government. When these

half-breeds made claims to the present government their claims were submitted to a commission and settled, with the result that these half-breeds are loyal and contented citizens of the Dominion. In the old days these half-breeds had claims, they sent these claims to the Dominion government, the Dominion government pigeon-holed them or threw them into the waste-paper basket and the result was that we had a serious rebellion in the Northwest Territories which cost between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000, to say nothing of the scores of bright young lives which were given up in the service of the country on that occasion. There is something in the association of the ideas and the association of ideas is so strong in this case that I must be pardoned for having brought this item to the attention of the House. The next item is engraving maps of the Dominion and Northwest Territories, $14,096.53. We know how this has increased the knowledge of the Dominion both within the confines of Canada and beyond them. It is part of that advertising which is bringing such rich results in men and money. Hon. gentlemen will not complain of that. Department of Labour-and now I come to some more of that charming campaign literature-$20,471.54. Will hon. gentlemen say they do not want the Department of Labour ? Will they say that if they came into power they would abolish the Department of Labour ? I think not. They dare not do it, however much they might wish to and I do not say they wish to. I have here pamphlet No. 8, headed ' Starvation Wages.' Then follows a schedule of the wages paid on the Intercolonial Railway that hon. gentlemen opposite say are not enough, and that the government think also are not enough, for since the time that those wages were paid they have increased them. This is another example of the hypocrisy of hon. gentlemen opposite in claiming that the expenditure is too great because here is an item in regard to which they want to make it still more. I do not complain so much of that as I do of this which is only second to that pamphlet from which I quoted a short time ago headed ' .Junketing Ministers.' In this pamphlet, No. 8, these hon. gentlemen say :
And this is the government that says the workingmen should be grateful to it because it is paying a ' minister of labour ' $8,000 a year !
Hon. gentlemen opposite very well know the miserable insinuation contained in that clause and the absolute falsity that lies within the four corners of that half truth. They surely know that the Minister of Labour is also the Postmaster General, that ns Postmaster General he draws exactly the salary which his Conservative predecessor, as Postmaster General drew, and that in addition to the salary of the Postmaster Mr. A. T. THOMPSON.
General he does not draw one single cent of pay for the immensely increased amount of labour which he in his generous anxiety for the good of the labouring classes has taken upon his shoulders.
Marconi wireless, $10,000. We led in assisting that young man to whom the great universities of the old world are now stretching forth a hand and upon whom they are showering honours and conferring degrees. We took him in when he was more friendless than he is now and gave him financial aid. His method has proved to be immensely valuable beyond peradventure, and we in Canada have the honour of having been in the forefront in assisting in the development of this modern wonder of science from which we will reap substantial financial benefits far beyond our investment. We have contributed $60,000 toward the Ottawa Improvement fund. Who will cavil at that 1 Not hon. gentlemen opposite. Sir, that vote of the money of the people of Canada for the improvement of Canada's capital is an outward and visible proof that Canada is no longer a number of isolated provinces experimentally strung together by a British Act of parliament, but that Canada is a united nation from ocean to ocean and from the southern boundary to the Artie sea, one and indivisable. Who will abject to the beautifying of our capital as the capitals of all other countries are beautified at the general expense of the people ? For the consolidation of the statutes we spent $12,722.08. Who will say, especially those in the legal profession, that that expenditure has been made before its time ? Alaskan boundary commission, $59,993. That is an expenditure-I may perhaps be pardoned for saying it-on a necessary evil. Hon. gentlemen will be surprised to learn that also in this delightful literature which has furnished us with so much instruction and amusement, the visit of the hon. Minister of the Interior to England last summer, where he worked, as, I suppose few men have ever worked in the interests of Canada, is actually put under the heading * junketing tours.' What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker ? A junketing tour.	That important mission of the
hon. the Minister of the Interior classed as one of the junketing tours ! These sums taken together reach a total of $269,193.14 and by tracing out other and smaller items I could very easily account for the small balance of $60,000. but I shall not attempt to do so as I do not desire to detain the House. Then, upon the Yukon provisional district the government had to provide $807,806.89 that hon. gentlemen did not have to provide, but the Yukon has paid for itself so that nothing is lost by the people of Canada.
Now, I am glad to say that I take up my last bundle of notes, which I shall pass

over as rapidly as possible. The increase in the expenditure on account of the collection of customs was $311,396.32. Is any one surprised at this increase. Frankly, I am very much surprised at the smallness of it, because I notice that we have collected $19,361,260.90 more than hon. gentlemen opposite collected in 1895, that we have actually collected in excess of their collection more than the whole sum which they gathered in customs revenue with an increased expenditure of only $311,396.32. It follows also that while the expenditure in 1895 was $5.13 per $100 of revenue collected, it was only $3.31 per $100 of revenue collected in 1903 by this government. There was an increased expenditure upon excise of $7,119.41, while there was an increase in revenue of $4,208,046.29. Comment is unnecessary in that, although I believe hon. gentlemen opposite are very much concerned to find that they have to pay a little more for their smoking tobacco than they did in the good old days of Tory rule. I do not wonder that they made tobacco cheap in those days. The people had to have a sedative. They were restless. Cheap tobacco was a necessity, but, when we have our pockets full of money we are prepared to pay a little more, we do not resent paying a little more for our tobacco and cigars and we are glad to know that this small increase, which is a considerable increase in the aggregate, is being expended on public works which will be of immense advantage to the people of Canada.
And so while our smoke goes upwards we can see through it as through a glass, darkly, public buildings springing up all through Canada as the result of this expenditure. I am not asking that the price of my smoking material be decreased one jot or tittle. Then, for weights and measures, electric light, and gas, the expenditure in 1895 was $98,173.67 and in 1903 it was $121,575.02, an increase of $23,401,35 ; an increase accounted for by the increased amount of inspecting done in Canada, and indeed I may mention that for some of this increased expenditure we get back an increased revenue. In the expenditure for culling timber there has been a decrease of $6,921; it is unnecessary to comment on that. For the inspection of staples, there is an increase of $63,906.46. But we have added a chief inspector of hides, an inspector of binder twine, and a rattling good one at that; two chief inspectors and several assistants for the inspection of grain, and a warehouse commissioner at Winnipeg. The growing commercial interests of the country, and the increased services demand of the government to meet these growing interests in this regard, that is ample to afford justification for this expenditure. In the matter of the inspection nnd tests to provide against adulteration of food, there is a decreased expenditure of $4,443.31, for which we claim no credit.
Then we come to the post office service, and it shows an increase of $511,531.01. In 1895 the Conservatives spent on the post office service $3,593,647.47 and in 1903 the Liberal government spent on the post office service $4,105,178.18. If there is one thing in Canada which the people now understand it is the magnificent record of this government in connection with the administration of the Post Office Department. The people are so thoroughly acquainted with the splendid administration of that department now, that it absolves me from the duty of explaining this increase. It is an increase of more than half a million dollars, but against that we have an increased revenue from the post office of $1,605,042.87, in spite of the fact that we have a two cent rate of postage where the Conservatives charged three cents for a letter. We have wiped out the old post office yearly deficit of about three-quarters of a million dollars, and we have a surplus in its place of more than one-quarter million dollars. We have, as I stated, a two cent postage rate instead of a three cent postage rate : we have better pay fori the employees ; better service for all ; and we have increased, not before it was time, the salaries of the postmasters throughout Canada.
Then with regard to the expenditure on public works. In 1895 the Conservatives spent $151,698.22, and in 1903 the Liberals spent $562,403.51 an increase of $410,705.29. This is quite a large item but of this amount I find that no less than $281,391.87 was spent on the telegraph lines in the Yukon, and we have already seen that the Yukon has practically cost this country nothing. Then, a large part of the balance of the increase is accounted for by the extension of land and cable telegraph lines in the lower St. Lawrence, where every effort is very properly being made to improve the condition of navigation. I point this out to the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) as one of the increases, and I think he will agree with me in saying that it is a very useful expenditure and not an extravagant one.
Then for the cost of collection of revenue on railways and canals ; there is an increase of $3,517,578.65, the largest increase of all. But let me point out that the revenue from the same sources has increased $3,347,131.52, in spite of a falling off in the canal revenues of $109,676.57, consequent upon the abolition of toils ; an abolition made in the interests of commerce, and but for which there would practically be no increased expense at all in this item, as otherwise the increased receipts would balance the increased expenditure. I need say nothing of the greater facilities which this increased expenditure has given to the merchants of Canada, resulting in an increase of wealth out of all proportion to the net loss on the expenditure. Then in regard

to minor revenues, there Is an increase of $1,073.01 which is a small item and which 1 only mention for the sake of completeness in dealing with the subject. In Dominion lands, there has been an increase of $56,028.30. I do not think we need be very shamefaced over this modest increase, in view of the fact that our income from this source has increased since 1895 by the tidy sum of $1,527,722.05. Then we come to trade and commerce, and there is an increase of $19,619.18 only, in spite of the fact that our foreign trade has increased from $224,420,485 to $407,001,494. Surely, in view of such a showing we need not be ashamed of that increase.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I have come to the end of my remarks, and I will ask you whether there is anything surprising in the fact, that after the careful study which I have made of these statistics. I have come to the decision to vote with pleasure in support of a government which is enterprising without being extravagant, and economical without being parsimonious.

The hon. gentleman from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) has accomplished a very great feat. He has gone through about 305 items, and extracted from about 305 pages of paper probably 365 ideas ; although, what bearing they may have upon the subject we are discussing I fail to see. The practice of the present administration is, that no minister ever defends his department, and that some volunteer has to be pressed into service when defence is offered. The hon. gentleman from Haldimand has done better than all the other volunteers, because he has defended in his own way-I won't say much about the way-not one department but every department of the administration. The hon. gentleman has shown us in this year of grace 19(44, what a real independent member of parliament is. He announced that he was an independent, and it is well that he mentioned it, because any one that has followed his record would never have dreamed it. I do not know that we could expect him to be independent.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He is one of the government whips.

It is not a question of government whips at all. but I think that the plums which have fallen into the mouth of that hon. gentleman are quite sufficient to guarantee his ceaseless support of the government for all time to come ; at least so long as the Liberal party is in power.
I am satisfied.
Y"ou are probably better satisfied than your supporters are. The hon. gentleman is perfectly satisfied with himself.
I am satisfied with the government.

I do not think I ever knew a gentleman who seemed more perfectly satisfied with himself than the hon. member from Haldimand, but the trouble is that the gentlemen who sit on his side of the House are not nearly so satisfied with him as we are. He endeavoured to be amusing but he was not amusing to his friends, although he was to us. Let me remind him that there is a broad distinction between expenditure and extravagance and that when we speak of extravagance we are not uecessarily speaking of large expenditure. So long as expenditure is in the interest of the people we will not complain, but when it descends to reckless extravagance and to squandering the resources of the country to secure votes to bolster up the government, then we on this side of the House do complain. The hon. member for Haldimand said that the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) was inconsistent in complaining, of extravagance while asking for a larger expenditure on the geological survey. The hon. gentleman does not understand the question. What the member for Toronto said is ; that we want rapid development in this country, and if that can be obtained by geological surveys it would be a wise expenditure to strengthen that branch of the public service. It is the same thing with reference to the wages paid to the employees on the Intercolonial Railway. We believe that an honest day's work deserves an honest day's wage, and the Conservative party will stand up, as it always has, for the application of that principle to the working classes of this country.
What wages did you pay the employees on the Intercolonial Railway?
The hon. gentleman will get a chance to speak when I sit down.
Why don't you answer that question ?

I don't even hear the hon. gentleman. The Conservative party is the party which always took care that there should be fair remuneration for the labour classes in Canada. It was the Conservative party that organized in 1878, that policy which gave employment to the labouring people of Canada, and afforded the means of paying them fair wages.
The hon. gentleman who has been endeavouring to discuss the public questions of the day, although with no great degree of success, referred to what the hon. member for West Toronto had said in reference to our not yet having obtained all the improvements we desire on the St. Lawrence route, and told us that was a pretty encouragement for immigration and a poor class of literature to disseminate in Great Britain. These hon. gentlemen ought to understand that question pretty well. If

they will search the records for eighteen years subsequent to 1878, when the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of Minister of Trade and Commerce was the chief spokesman or chief writer of the party, they will find the kind of encouragement he gave to people to come to this country. They will find that that hon. gentleman did all he could to prevent people coming by spreading broadcast not only through Great Britain but through the United States literature calculated to discourage immigration to Canada in the most effectual way. The hon. member for Haldi-mand complains of some literature that he got in some way. I hope he got it honestly. 1 hope he did not steal it, because they are awfully down on stealing on that side of the Hpuse. I hope too that it will do him some good. But I notice that he has not fully grasped the meaning of that literature. He chooses an isolated sentence, and fails to convey to the House any idea of its meaning. He complains that Mr. Sifton's visit to England should have been spoken of as a junketing tour. Well, X do not think the expression is a happy one. It was at the time parliament was in session that Mr. Sifton was in England and the Minister of Agriculture in Japan, and in consequence we in the House of Commons found it impossible to get a good deal of the information we wanted from time to time from the responsible ministers of the Crown. But I do not think it should be called a junketing expedition. I think we might better call it a pot-latch, which is an Indian term, and no doubt the hon. member for Haldimand is familiar with the Indian language ; for undoubtedly, so far as we can learn, it was a complete and thorough give-way feast on the part of our representatives. The hon. gentleman took a position which I am afraid will destroy his chance of reward for some time to come. It is the unhappy fate of most of the extreme advocates of the government's position never to be rewarded. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who I am sorry is not in his usual form at present, is a conspicuous instance of how extremists are never rewarded. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, with ' whom I sympathize^ is another instance of how the most pronounced and vigorous extremists never come to their reward.
His family gets it.

But that does not compensate him for the fact that in the formation of the cabinet he was overlooked, and that the coveted prize to which he had been looking forward for many years was passed over to the hon. gentleman now sitting beside him, the hon. Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Haldimand has gone so far beyond what is reasonable in defending the government that I am afraid that if another junketing expedition is made to England, he will not be selected to join
it, even if his party continues in power, which is not likely. The hon. gentleman protests too much ; he announces too much; in fact, he says too much in every respect. From the beginning to the end of His speech he boasts of the enormous expenditure of this government, as contrasted with that of the former ad-ministration-which must have been a source of great pain to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, who denounced any advance in the expenditure, and proclaimed that a retrograde movement should be made in the direction of economy and retrenchment, and said that that would prevail if the Reform party got into power. The hon. gentleman tells us of an expenditure by the present administration of $16.000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway, and of $18,000,000 upon the development of our water-ways. That is just where the shoe pinches at the present time. Under a wise and statesmanlike policy of transportation for this country, definitely mapped out, and carried on judiciously, a large expenditure may be justified. But when hon. gentlemen do as this cabinet has done-rush headlong into expenditures, and then suddenly change their whole line of policy, and, instead, of developing the traffic of the west through central Canada to our own ocean ports, put it under the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company-then the more they say about that policy under which they spent about $35,000,000 or more, the greater is their condemnation. The hon. gentleman boasted too of railway subsidies. 1 think he may well boast. While he was talking, I looked at the index of 1 Hansard ' of last year, and I found under the heading of subsidies more than eighty subjects classified as being subsidized last session. I think hon. gentlemen opposite have goue mad in the matter of subsidies. Instead of the hon. member for Haldimand boasting of the amount they have spent on subsidies, it would be well for him to call on the government to halt in this matter if they expect to retain their seats, because the people will not stand this subsidy business much longer. As an illustration of the way it works out, I may state that a little while ago the Dominion government granted a money subsidy to the James Bay Railway of $1,500,000. The company went to the Ontario government and got a guarantee of $5,000,000. Immediately after the close of the recent session of the Ontario legislature we had the announcement that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, reviled as it is by hon. gentlemen who support the government, is going to build a parallel line between the same termini without asking a dollar of assistance of any kind from either the Dominion or the Ontario government. This shows that this matter of subsidies is one that requires immediate attention, and I am very much mistaken if the people of Canada do not attend to it at the next general election, whenever
*
