hon. gentlemen opposite have the courage to bring that election on.
The hon. gentleman referred to the iron and steel bounties and the lead bounty, but not to the shipping bounty. He did not tell us, of course, that the other day a government official went to Collingwood to ascertain the value of dry-dock facilities, said to have been constructed there by certain gentlemen of that town, and that he valued these at $500,000, and that we are now paying, and will pay for twenty years to come, a subsidy of $15,000 per year as a bounty to that industry alone. And should the present government be returned again to power, no doubt the same gentlemen will exercise the same power over the government as they have been doing lately. How they managed it, I do not know. But the hon. gentleman from North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy) seems to be able to bring this government to book in some peculiar way, and I wish him luck when he goes to Oro and Vespra and the other townships round about and explains how it has come to pass that these sums are paid by the government into the lap of Collingwood. He is another Independent, and the ways of these independents on that side are past finding out. I am not in harmony with the hon. gentleman when he boasts of these bounties. I remember when not only supporters of the present government outside the cabinet, but even ministers now in the cabinet, taught us that of all subventions, bounties and subsidies were the most odious abominations of protection. I do not know what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) would say now, but I heard him say a couple of years ago that there was no use talking about this dumping business because you could not do anything with it by means of a tariff or a bounty, and that on the other hand it was a blessing in disguise-very thickly disguised I always thought. That, however, was his view then. Hon. gentlemen opposite are fond of taking up the statements of members on this side and holding them out as the policy of the opposition. Well, as I understand it, the opposition policy is the one which our leader announces. It is a policy with which we are in harmony, or it would not be announced. But individual members on this side may express their independent views without committing the party to them. In anything I say in the House, unless it be something on which our leader has pronounced a policy, I am simply enunciating my own views, and I want to put on record here and now my opposition to the scheme of bounties and bonuses and subsidies in Canada. I listened to the glowing language -and it was more glowing than sensible describing the illimitable resources of Canada. I heartily agree with him. But if Canada has such a fertile soil for the teeming populations of other countries, if it offers such a productive field for Mr. LENNOX.
immigration, if it has mines and minerals and fisheries, if its agricultural resources are so great, and if our growing trade and commerce requires greater facilities for the handling of its traffic, then the time has come when we do not need to subsidize these various industries in order that they may live. I am straight and square in favour of adequate protection, or, if you have any better term than ' adequate protection, ' you may substitute it. I am in favour of such duties as will protect our people in the various ranks of industrial life, but I am opposed to subventions and subsidies and devices of that knid. I believe that they are unfair and unequal. They are not fair to one of the great classes, at all events, which should be protected and cared for and whose .rights should be respected in this country. But before I deal specifically with that subject, let me refer for a moment or two to other matters to which the hon. gentleman has referred. He talked of exhibitions aud an hon. gentleman beside me suggests that he made an exhibition of himself. I am not disposed, however, to be severe on the hon. gentleman in his absence. He did not remain to hear the other side, but hastened out of the chamber after he made his speech, and no doubt he remembered the old line He who fights and runs away May live to fight another day.
If our exhibitions generally are conducted on the same lines as the one of which we have had an explanation from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) the other day-. I refer to the permanent exhibition connected with the Colonial Institute which, the minister was compelled to admit, was under charge of the Home Department of Trade and Commerce, into which is thrown every-tliing that nobody else will have anything to do with, and in that respect resembles the Department of Agriculture in Canada- the less we have of them decidedly the better for the people.
With regard to immigration, the hon. gentleman showed that there is no field in the world so favourable for industrial pursuits to-day as Canada, and for those who are seeking permanent homes were they will be comfortably off, the resources of Canada offer inducements to be found nowhere else. In these remarks I entirely concur and am prepared to say that we are to-day receiving back a large portion of those whom the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his-colleagues succeeded in driving from Canada from 1878 to 1896. Now when we have a loyal opposition which does not defame the country, but extols its advantages, which is loyally endeavouring to support the government where it can, we ought to have a larger immigration ; and I venture to say that had it not been for the unfair and disloyal utterances of hon. gentlemen opposite when in opposition, our population would be double to-djiy what it is.

My hon. friend from Haldimand did not tell 'us anything about these little harbours at the mouths of creeks.- I am going to spend a little time In classifying that expenditure, and showing how much money we have frittered away upon public works where there is no justification for the expenditure of even a single dollar-unless it can be a justification by a government to show that they have spent money for the purpose of keeping themselves in power. No one who has followed the discussion of the estimates in this House during the last three or four years can fail to know that in the record there are abundant instances of such expenditure. X do not intend to go into those instances now ; but, before the session closes, I intend to show what the expenditures have been in these cases wherQ there was no justification in the public in terest, 'but where the only object of the expenditure was to offer a sop to a locality to win its favour for the government.
The hon. gentleman Mr. A. T. Thompson! spoke of superannuation. But he did not tell us the important fact that superannuations were made by this government for the purpose of making places for their followers. For that purpose they have superannuated a great number of men who were more capable than are their successors in oflice. Ho says that no superannuation system Obtains now. The hon. gentleman has a bad memory. X think that I remember that last session he himself spoke in favour of the increase of judges' salaries and of the change in the superannuation of judges. What the hon. gentleman means is that if the superannuation is of some civil servant who has been drawing $800, or $1,000, or $1,200 a year, it is an iniquity, but if it is to superannuate a gentleman who has drawn for twenty-five or thirty years a salary of $5,000 or $0,000 a year, then it is a virtue which he will commend. I am not quite in accord with him in that view. There was one remarkable thing about the hon. gentleman's speech, and that is that he talked of everything but the budget. I think he is to be commended for that. I am going to do pretty nearly the same, because there is mighty little to talk about if one confines himself to the budget. The budget has been a vanishing spectacle year by year. W hen I entered this House four years ago and heard my first budget, I thought it was a pretty weak performance-except in the matter of congratulation. That congratulation has been the main point of the budget ever since. But in everything else it has grown weaker year by year, more mixed and muddled year by year. It would be difficult for any hon gentleman to make a speech if he confined himself to that budget, particularly would it be difficult for a supporter of the government. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House can at least deal with the budget as a negative quantity ; they can criticise it for what it does not contain rather than for
what it does. Even when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) spoke he had to steer clear of the budget-not for lack of ability, for I do not believe anything of that kind-but through lack of material. He had to abandon the budget and take up one of his old speeches delivered on former occasions in this House. However Interesting it was as a reminiscence, still, though he gave it with vigour, it had not at all the effect of novelty. He used about the same language and brought in his points in about the same order as on former occasions.
Now, I have a word or two to say with regard to the proposal of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to grant a bounty of H cents a gallon upon the production of crude oil. I have already said that I am absolutely opposed to the principle of bounties. Bounties serve no purpose except to enrich the few at the expense of the many. They cannot effect the object the hon. minister says he desires. And the hon. gentleman does not think they will effect that object- and X can demonstrate that in a moment. He says that we produced crude oil last year to the amount of over 16,000,000 gallons, and he tells us he is putting on the bounty in order to increase the production of crude oil, so that the refiners may have more employment than before. But when he tries to figure out what his bounty of li cents per gallon will cost, on what does he base his calculation ? Why, on something over 16,000,000 gallons-showing that he does not expect a single gallon of increased production by reason of this bounty that he is offering. The hon. gentleman knows that he is giving a sop to the Standard Oil Company, and wiping out this industry which he is professing to serve. I am opposed to bounties and in favour of adequate protection to all our industries, a protection which will work out so that each industry will be protected in the same degree. In another way the Finance Minister is most misleading in the calculation he puts before the people as to this bounty of 14 cents per gallon on crude oil. He gave us to understand that the people would pay 14 cents per gallon more on coal oil. But, as a matter of fact, it will be 3 cents a gallon on coal oil, because it takes two gallons of crude oil to make one gallon of burning fluid. Did not the bon. gentleman (Mr Fielding) know that, or did he not want to tell the people the truth and the whole truth with regard to this matter ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the bounty be paid on the crude or on the refined V
It will be paid on the crude.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why, then, should the calculation be made on the refined ?

For this reason-that the people do not burn crude oil, but refined

oil. But lion, gentlemen opposite probably think that the people should burn something else. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thompson) thought, if I understood him aright, that the tallow dip was good enough for the common people. Perhaps the Minister of Finance thinks that unrefined oil would be good enough for the hulk of the people in the country. The cost of his bounty will be 3 cents a gallon on the refined oil.
Now, I am requested to read for the benefit of the House what the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) said. I have here the Ottawa ' Free Press ' of this day

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is that a Liberal paper ?
I believe so.
The Liberal organ in this city.

The ' Free Press ' says :
It was a reminder of the days when Sir Richard dealt his blows with the force of a mental giant and when every blow left its mark on the adversary. The havoc he wrought with those blows of his explains why Sir Richard is not very popular on the opposition side of the House to-day.
That is enough for an introduction. 1 think you will say that,they are doing him justice-unless they are making him ridiculous. The ' Free Press ' goes on :
Be that as it may, Sir Richard had been charged with having been recusant to free trade, but he was able to show that the idea was a figment of the imagination. He had never in his life been a free trader.
As a protectionist he had taken part in the campaign of 1878, and he had championed the cause on every hustings from that day to this.
Sir Richard made avowal that he had once delivered a lecture on speculative free trade, but in the opening paragraph he had expressly declared that it had no reference to practical free trade as a policy for Canada.
Surely there was no apostacy to principle here. And then came the pungent drollery, the caustic humour with which he showed how first one and then another on the opposition side, who had at an earlier period of their life appeared on free trade platforms assailing protection as the Scottish Calvinists used to assail the papacy, and forsaken the faith to which they had pledged themselves.
Now I shall read a few lines here from an excellent authority :
A bounty is merely the means of making a present to the manufacturer at the expense of the people at large. It creates no wealth iri the country. It is a means of transferring money from the pocket of one man to the pocket of another : it is a means of compelling the people generally to enhance the profits of the manufacturer, to put into his pocket money that he never earned.
I would be very sorry to nave it understood by the great agricultural classes of this country, I was in favour of bounties in any Mr. LENNOX.
shape or form. I am not in favour of them, because I recognize that the system is unfair to the great agricultural class of this country.
I have heard nothing which is better sense or more concise than the statement made in this passage by the hon. member for South Simcoe at the last session and so I have read it to the House. I think it will be received as containing a very considerable amount of wisdom.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. A. T. Thompson) spoke on every available subject, except the interest of the rural constituency which he represents. I want to say that although it may be in the interest of some classes to have a bounty imposed, to be taken out of the pockets of the people, yet it can never be in the interest of the great agricultural class of this country, and whatever other interest we may be able to serve, I for one, so long as I represent a rural constituency, aye, and even if I should represent a city constituency, will feel that the first interest to be considered in this country, having due regard to all other interests as well, is the interest of agriculture.
At six o'clock House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

The budget debate always excites a great deal of interest not only in this House but also in the country. It is, I suppose, the most important debate we ever have had in parliament. It is time, I think I may say, of stock taking, a time when we review the affairs of the country for the past year and make an estimate of those affairs for the coming year. By that means we ascertain where we are, where we stand, whether we are progressing or retrograding. Any man who does not at a certain time of the year take stock of his affairs to find out whether he is going ahead or behind, is not a good business man. So in parliament if we do not as a nation take stock once a year and ascertain how we are standing, we are not conducting the affairs of the country as we should. The budget speech which was delivered the other day has excited great interest throughout the country. It was one of the most important speeches that has ever been delivered in this House. It must he exceedingly gratifying to the people of this country to read the record of the progress and advancement of this Dominion of Canada. The gentlemen to your left who have preceded me have found it a very hard road to travel, and their speeches have been the shortest that I have ever listened to in a budget debate. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) occupied only twenty-five or thirty minutes. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) hardly came up to

that time ; in about twenty five minutes he said all he could say. It is an evidence that they can find very little to criticise in the position of the country and the manner in which its affairs have been conducted in the past year. One can scarcely credit the state of affairs that has been revealed by the Finance Minister. If we did not know it was true, we could scarcely realize that this Dominion is making such tremendous progress as it has been making within the last few years. The story of the extraordinary advancement of this Dominion reads almost like a fairy tale, and is exceedingly gratifying to every well wisher of the country. There are two ways in which we can ascertain the progress of a country, just as in the case of an individual. If a merchant or a farmer or a trader is increasing his sales from year to year, selling more goods, doing a greater business, it is an evidence that he is prospering and is adding to his estate, and so with a nation. We find_ that this Dominion has made wonderful progress within the last few years when compared with the record of previous years. What we buy and what we sell is of great interest to us. I remember that when our Conservative friends were in power, they boasted very often of the progress the country was making. They pointed to an increase in the trade of this Dominion of $3,500,000 per year. That was the average during the eighteen years they were in power. The trade of this country increased from $172,000,000 in 1878 to $229,000,000 in 1896, an increase of $66,000,000 or about $3,-
500,000	per year.
It is a matter of record that our hon. friends on the Conservative side were exceedingly gratified with the progress that had been made. If you look over the speeches of the late Minister of Finance you will find that he pointed with pride and satisfaction to the record of the increased trade of the country as an evidence of a wise administration of the affairs of the country under his rule. Now. Sir, taking that as a criterion, we may judge of the progress of the country during the seven years that it has been under the guidance of the Liberal party, and we find that the trade of the country increased from $239,000,000 in 1896 to no less a sum than $467,000,000 in 1903, that the trade of the country increased not at the rate of $3,500,000 a year, but at the rate of nearly $32^ 000,000 a year. 1 think that if we look with pride and gratification to the fact that under the regime of our Conservative friends the foreign trade of this country was increased by $3,500,000 a year it must be exceedingly gratifying to them now to find that that trade has gone up to the extent of about $32,000,000 a year. We find also that the increase in trade has been largely in Canadian products! We find rthat the total exports of Canadian products for the seven
years previous to the advent of the Liberal administration, from 1890 to 1896. were, in round numbers $696*000,0001 Comparing that with the last seven years of the Liberal administration, from 1897 to 1903, we find that the total exports of Canadian products were $1,166,000,000, or an increase In these seven years over the previous seven years when the Conservative party ruled, of no less than $470,000,000. You can hardly realize that that $470,000,000 has gone into the pockets largely of the farmers and producer of this country.
It is interesting to ascertain how this increase has occurred. We find that of products of the miue, from 1890 to 1896. we exported $42,730,000. During the last seven years this was increased to $170,000,000, or an increase in these seven years over the previous seven years of $127,000,000. Then, we have the fisheries. Our exports of the products of the fisheries for the seven years previous to 1896 were $69,468,000. During the latter seven year period they Increased to $78,898,000. or an increase in these seven years of about $9,000,000. Of the products of the forest the exports increased from $176,000,000 during the first seven year period to $213,000,000 during the last seven year period, or an increase of $37,000,000. Then we come to the products of the farm. The exports of the products of the farm show a wonderful increase, an increase from $331,000,000 for the previous seven years to no less than $573,000,000 for the last seven years, or an increase of $240,000,000 for the last seven years over the previous seven years. Then, I am also glad to know that the exports of manufactures have increased from $51,000,000 to $100,000,000 or an increase of $50,000,000. These facts are exceedingly gratifying to us. They show that our products are being sold to good advantage and that we are reaping enormous profits from them.
If we examine the list of exports we find that we can pick out some items in that trade of particular interest to the farmers of this country. We find that the exports of butter rose from $6,140,000 during the seven years previous to 1896 to nearly $29,000,000 during the last seven years, or an increase of $22,000,000. Then, take cheese. The exports of cheese during the seven years previous to 1896 amounted to $87,000,000. whereas, for the last seven years they amounted to $133,978,000, or an increase of $46,000,000 in that one article alone. We may take hams, bacon, and pork, the exports of which increased from $15,-
572,000	to $77,558,000 or an increase of $62,000,000.
It is well to ask the reason why it is that we have made such astonishing progress in these lines, that we have been able to sell so much more of these goods during the last seven years than we were dur-

ing tlie previous seven years. Tlie rain fell and the sun shone, during the first seven years the same as during the last seven years. The crops grew and Providence blessed this country during the seven years between 1890 and 1896 the same as Providence has blessed this land from 1897 to 1903 and it is interesting to know how it is that we have made such wonderful progress and that we have been able to sell so much more in the last seven years than we were in the seven years previously. It is an advantage to have added to the wealth of this country the enormous sum of money that has gone into the pockets of the people. Our hon. friends say, as they have been saying to-day, that this is largely owing to Providence. They give no credit to the government of this country at all, but I think a little investigation will show that under the wise direction of this government the farmers have been enabled to take advantage of the opportunities presented to them in very many ways. For instance, let me point to a few of the reasons why this increase has taken place. We all remember that when the government took charge of the affairs of this country in 1896 our cattle could not go into the United States without being quarantined for a certain length of time at the border. What was the result of that ? In the four and a half years during which that quarantine was in force we only sent to the United States 3,762 head of cattle at a valuation of $52,000, in round numbers. What did this government do ? The Hon. Sydney A. Fisher, the practical businesslike intelligent farmer who was placed at the head of the Department of Agriculture, a man who knew what this country demanded, a man who understood what the farmers wanted, a man who realized the responsibilities of his position, immediately set himself to work to effect a remedy. With the Hon. John Dryden, Minister of Agriculture in the province of Ontario, he went to Washington and there, like business men, they brought this matter to the attention of the American government, the state of affairs was explained and by bringing their business ability to bear upon the authorities at Washington, they secured the removal of this quar-antine that had proved so disastrous to the interests of the farmers of Canada. What was the result in the next four and a half years ? In the next four and a half years after the quarantine was removed instead of sending 3,762 head of cattle to the United States, we sent no less than 349,393 at a valuation not of $52,000, but at a valuation, getting it back in good Canadian money, of no less than $5,329,000. Will any man say that that was not one act which contributed largely to the welfare of the great agricultural classes of this country? Ever since, the exportation to the United States of our cattle has been going on. We have Mr. CAMPBELL.
a great many cattle that we cannot send across the ocean. It does not pay to send them 3,000 miles to market. We find that in the great cities of the United States, such as New York and Boston, where there are millions and millions of people, a market for these cattle, and the result is that the farmers of this country sent in four and a half years after these quarantine restrictions were removed no less than 349,000 head of cattle at a valuation of $5,329,000.
The system of cold storage, brought to perfection by this government, has also contributed in a large degree to our prosperity because before cold storage was brought to a successful development our perishable produce could not be sent to the markets of the world in proper condition. The late government started with a crude system of cold storage, filling the steamers with ice that was melted before the vessels got to the ocean, with the result that the goods arrived in the old country in a worse condition than they were in when they started on the voyage. Under the present Minister of Agriculture, who understands' his business, the cold storage system was perfected. He first established the system on the railways throughout the Dominion, giving the railway companies a bonus to induce them to fit up their cars so that the perishable products could be carried from the farmers' door to the world's markets. Then, cold storage warehouses were erected in Montreal, and the minister made arrangements with the steamship companies to fit up mechanical appliances in their vessels so that our products could be properly cared for on the ocean voyage. In the first year of the experiment, 17 ocean steamers fitted with cold storage sailed from Montreal, and last year there were 35 steamers so fitted. Last year there were 144 sailings from the port of Montreal alone, of ships furnished with mechanical cold storage of the most modern and approved type. As the result of these experiments, the export of our butter and cheese and poultry and eggs has enormously increased; and the farmers have been enabled to realize a higher price than heretofore. That has contributed in large degree to the prosperity of the farmers of Canada. That is the reason why our farmers got $470,000,000 more for their products in the last seven years than they did before. But that it not all. The Minister of Agriculture established in ail the provinces of this Dominion dairying schools to edjicate the people in the best methods of manufacturing butter and cheese. Our exports of butter have largely increased, but we are yet only at the beginning of that trade. There is a market in the old country for ten times the quantity of butter we now export, and with a continuation of the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture we hope to capture that market.

Some people may say that while our products have increased, the people of Canada have not got the money, but let us see how that pans out. Is not this a pretty sure criterion. In 1878 the deposits in the banks of this country amounted to $79,000,000, and in 1896 they amounted to $245,000,000, an increase in eighteen years of $165,831,000. But what has been the story since 1896? Instead of having $245,000,000 on deposit in the banks as we had then, the people of Canada had in the year 1903 no less than $461,000,000, or an increase in these seven years of $216,000,000 against an increase of only $165,000,000 during the long eighteen years of Tory rule. That is remarkable progress. It redounds largely to the credit of this government of wise and practical men, who oy the methods they have adopted to encourage and facilitate the manufacture and transportation of our pi'oducts, added to the general prosperity of the Dominion. Another test we might make, can be taken from the post office returns. The correspondence of a prosperous and progressive nation is constantly increasing. The postal record shows us that in 1878 we posted 44,000,000 letters ; in 1896 116,000.000 letters, or an increase in eighteen years of 72,000.000 letters. But what has been the wonderful record since 1896 ? Last year we posted 235,000,000 letters, or an increase of 119,000.000 over 1896, as against an increase of only 72,000,000 in the eighteen years of Conservative government. These are strong, convincing, and indisputable proofs of the progress we have made.
And, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to know that the manufacturing interests of this Dominion, which we all know are a great factor in the welfare of a country, have shared in the general prosperity. Our manufacturing industries during the last seven years have made far more progress than during the eighteen years of Conservative rule. In 1896 we exported $9,365,000 worth of manufactured products, and in 1903 that rose to over $21,000,000 worth, an increase ia seven years of over $11,000,000 worth.
Compare that with the previous record, from 1878 to 1896. The increase was only a little over $5,000,000 in eighteen years under the national policy, which according to its advocates was going to build up this Dominion, which was designed especially for the benefit of the manufacturing interests oh Canada, which hon. gentlemen opposite have never ceased to laud and which they claim had laid the foundations, broad and deep, of the future prosperity of the manufacturing interests of this Dominion ; and yet under that national policy, during the eighteen years of its continuance, our exports of manufactured goods only increased $5,237,000. Since the abolition of the national policy, since the tariff was revised by practical men on business lines, the manufacturers of this Dominion have gone on
increasing by leaps and bounds, so that during the last seven years they have increased their exports by $11,259,000, against an increase of $5,000,000 under the national policy in eighteen years.
Now, I believe the manufacturing establishments of this Dominion should receive wise encouragement from the Dominion government. I think the welfare of this country largely depends on the success of its manufacturing establishments. You can see them in the neighbourhood of our towns and cities, employing from 500 to
1,000	men, adding to the population, increasing the value of land all round, giving value to the products of the farm, and the market garden. So I say it is a wise thing for the government to encourage the building up of manufacturing establishments in every way they possibly can ; and the revision of the tariff made in 1897 contributed in a large degree to the building up of the manufactures of this country and making them as prosperous as they are to-day.
Let me point out one or two ways in which the tariff has been revised. You can revise the tariff in such a way as to paralyze the industries of this Dominion. The government in 1897 went about their work in a businesslike way. They reduced the duties on the natural raw products of this country. Take, for instance, iron and steel, the great raw product that enters into the manufacture of every implement used on the farm, of every ship that sails on our seas, and of every railway train that passes over the land. Under the national policy which our Conservative friends have so lauded, this raw product, so necessary to the commercial life of the country, was taxed to the extent of about 60 per cent. This government came into power and cut that duty in two, with the result that our manufacturing establishments throughout this Dominion have been enlarging their plants, increasing their output, and sending their goods to all parts of the world. There is a factory in my own county which has doubled and trebled its production in the last seven years-the Dominion Radiator Company, of Toronto, which is now sending its goods to all parts of the wide world. Even the public buildings in far-off Russia are heated by radiators made in the city of Toronto. These works were not prospering under the old system, when they had to pay that enormous duty on their raw material. Their output was curtailed, they could not compete with other manufacturers, and they were not able to make a profit. But since then they have grown and have extended their works, until now their goods are going to all parts of the world. Take the Massey-Harris Company, who use from twenty-five to thirty tons of metal every day, paying an enormous duty upon it. They were handicapped and unable to send their goods abroad ; but as soon as the duty was reduced, they were able to compete with

their neighbours, enlarge their plant, double their output, employ double the number of men and largely Increase the wages of those men. They have grown and have extended their works until now the whole world is their market. And recently we have had the Deerlng Company established in the city of Hamilton, investing millions of capital, employing, X am told, 10,000 men, and prepared to manufacture agricultural implements and send them to all parts of the world. I could point in the same way to other manufacturing establishments. Go to Ottawa, Montreal, Hamilton, Peterborough, Halifax or anywhere else in this wide Dominion, and you will find that the manufacturing establishments have increased and prospered, doubled their output, and given employment to more men and at increased wages. I do not say that the tariff is perfect. I have thought that certain revisions of the tariff could be made, some reductions and possibly some increases, that would still further bring prosperity to our manufacturing establishments ; and X am glad to know that the government have wisely decided to give some redress by placing some goods on the free list, and thus placing the establishments in a better position to manufacture their product at a lower price than before, and to supply the consumers not only of Canada but of the wide world.
In this connection I might point to the revision of the coal oil duties. That seems to me to be a sensible change. At present we have five cents a gallon on refined oil and five cents a gallon on crude oil. It takes two gallons of crude oil to make one gallon of refined ; so that we have this anomaly, that there is a duty practically of ten cents a gallon on the raw product and only five cents a gallon on the finished article. In the revision of the tariff the sensible thing has been done ; the duty on the refined has been reduced to 2-1 cents a gallon, the benefit of which will be enjoyed by the consumers of oil throughout this Dominion ; and crude oil has been placed on the free list, which I hope and believe will result in every single gallon of the 16,000,000 gallons or whatever quantity of oil is used in Canada, being refined in the Dominion. Our refiners get their crude oil in free, and have 2i cents a gallon of protection on the refined. So that we will compel all the refiners of this Dominion, I believe, to refine the entire product of this Dominion in this country itself. That will give employment to double the quantity of men now engaged in that industry. We only produce in Canada one-half the quantity of oil we consume, so that if we refine the whole product in Canada, we will employ just about double the quantity of men and at the same time give the consumers their coal oil cheaper. Therefore I think that provision is wise and sensible and will promote the interests of the people.

The results of this development, the effect of the prosperous times we have had, brought about largely by the wise legislation of this government, are seen in another direction. We have an enormous territory in the Northwest, and what we require above all in Canada is people. It is almost incredible that in this great Dominion, so rich in natural products, mineral treasures and other resources, with the Canadian Pacific Railway running through from end to end and with branch lines extending in every direction-it is almost inconceivable that for ten years we did nothing but mark time and not only did not add to our population, but could not keep the immigration we brought in. Instead of there being in the country, the 860.000 people which the returns show were brought in previously to 1896, it was found that we had not retained our natural increase and that those whom we brought in had gone out of the country again to the United States. We found also in the eastern states Canadian boys and girls who had fled from this Dominion to the busy centres of trade on the other side of the line. At the head of the American banks and other great establishments, you will find Canadian boys, who had been born and raised and educated in Canada and had gone to this foreign country, and who, by their enterprise, ability, industry and integrity had raised themselves step by step until they had reached the highest positions. Was it not lamentable that all these bright young men and women should have been forced to leave our country ? and under the regulations which then existed, we find that in the decade previous to 1896, of the immigrants who had come in and who had cost this country a large amount, nearly all had gone to the United States. But when the present government came into power, under the wise administration of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton), who knew the situation and who knew the Northwest, a new departure was made. Immigration agents were sent not only to Europe but to the United States, to Michigan, Kansas, Dakota, Illinois and the western states, and by means of the literature they distributed and the information they were able to give, the stream of immigration was turned back again and every year since, that stream flowing into Canada has increased and continues to grow as the years roll on. What does the last year show ? Why, from 1890 to 1896, only 271,216 immigrants were brought into Canada, and the public returns of the census showed that these immigrants did not remain in Canada. But from 1897 to 1903 no less than 366,916 immigrants came into Canada, or an increase in those seven years of 95,730. In those seven years the settlers' effects that were brought in were nearly a million dolldrs more than they were in the previous seven years ? Our Conservative friends may say that those immigrants did

not remain in Canada, but we have a test which will show that they did. Take the returns of the homestead entries and what do we find ? In 1896 there were only 1,857, whereas in 1903 they amounted to 31,330. From 1890 to 1896, there were only 22,845 homestead entries, and in the last seven years they increased to 75,530, showing an increase of 52,685. Why, we increased the homestead entries more in the last seven years by nearly 13,000 than they amounted to in the whole eighteen years of Tory rule. We have proved conclusively that the immigrants we are now bringing in are remaining in the country and helping to build it up, and it is exceedingly gratifying to know that the class of immigrants we are getting is of the very best character. Last year 80 to 90 per cent of those who came were the very best class we could desire- from the United States, Great Britain and Scandinavia. The inferior class, which we do not desire, went to the United States. I think that this record of prosperity must be exceedingly gratifying to the people, and that the government, in adopting the regulations they have made, in the perfecting of the system of cold storage, and in the encouragement and improvement of the making of butter and cheese, have contributed to a great extent in bringing this about.
The government have also been wise in other directions. They have not confined their legislation to the farmers and manufacturers, but have been looking particularly after the interests of the great labour *and artisan classes. I say that the man who works behind the plough, the girl who sweeps out the office, are the class which any government should protect. They are the helpless ones who need aid, support and encouragement. The wealthy men and rich corporations can look after themselves, but the man who is alone in the field, the man who shoves the plane and guides the plough is the man the government should look after and protect. What has this government done in that direction ? One of the first things they did was to abolish the sweating-system. Of all the iniquities that ever disgraced the annals of any country, the most disgraceful, was the condition which existed under the late government in the sweating system. It has been proved beyond doubt by the commission which was appointed to investigate this system, that in Montreal and Toronto the big contractors who had secured contracts for supplying clothing to the militia and who were given big prices, sub-let those contracts to others, who in turn again sub-let them, and it was proven beyond a doubt that poor women in Montreal and Toronto were forced to work the whole day long making this clothing at the rate of 25 cents a day.
This great Dominion of Canada, though paying out large sums for the manufacture of these goods, did not regard the rights of the poor people, but neglected their interests and so enabled the contractors to fleece
them, to reduce their wages to a starvation level. This government at once abolished that system ; they provided that every contractor, no matter what his colour, nationality or creed might be, should pay the current rate of wages to every persou working on the job. Whether the co'ntract -was for the building of a post office, the construction of a wharf, dock or pier, the making of a railway, the digging of a canal or the manufacture of clothing required for the army and navy, every person engaged in the work must be paid the current rate of wages, whatever that might be. And so, this government has looked after the interests of those who, above all others needed the government's guidance and support and protection. I remember when, but a few years ago, a scandalous case arose which was discussed at some length in this House. The contractor who was building a railway- I think it was the Toronto, Hamilton and Burlington-sub-let his contract to an American. The American sub-contractor came over here, employed a large number of men, and set them to work on the railway. A progress estimate, was made of the work done, and the sub-contractor was given his pay, with which he cleared out, and not one of these men received from him pay for the work they had done. Some time after, application was made to this parliament for an amendment to the charter of the company. And, under this government, a stipulation was made that before that legislation was passed and the amendment made, a settlement had to be made with the men who had done the work on the railway but had not been paid for it. I remember another case in the western part of Ontario. The government let a contract, and the contractors sub-let the work, and the sub-contractors defrauded the men out of their wages. But this government stopped all that. Under the present system, they can say to the contractor :	It does not matter
to us whether you sublet your contract or not ; but if you do sublet it we will not pay you a single dollar until every man on the job has received his just wage. Is not that what a government ought to do ? It is to the credit of this government that they had this law enacted since they came into power and that they have carried it out so efficiently. Then, they have brought into force a Conciliation Act with a view to avoiding those strikes and lock-outs arising out of difficulties between manufacturers or contractors and their employees ; and I am glad to say that, under the efficient administration of the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) this Act has been the means of avoiding a great many strikes and settling a great many difficulties that would have been an injury both to the men and their employers. So, in these cases-and many more might be cited-the government have shown themselves to be progressive; they have moved forward with the times ; they have

not only protected and encouraged, as I said, the great agricultural classes and the manufacturing classes, but they have also looked after the rights and interests of the artisans and labourers, who so much need the assistance of the government.
Looking over the government's record, I cannot but believe that the tariff revision next year which they have announced will be one that will help the great industries of this country as well as the great body of consumers. The government have shown their ability in the past to solve the difficult questions involved in a tariff policy, and to do it in such a way as to bring about great prosperity to the Dominion. And so I believe that, when the revision of the tariff takes place next year, changes that are needed will be found to be wisely made. There are some articles the duty on which could be advantageously increased, while on * some others a reduction would be in the interest of the country. You can afford protection to manufacturers in either of two ways-by increasing the duties on what they manufacture, or reducing the duties on their raw material. A reduction of the cost of raw material enables them to sell their goods at lower prices than before, and so to increase their sales and relatively reduce the cost of their manufacture. This was largely the plan adopted by the government in 1897, and I feel sure that when the revision takes place next year it will be made on broad lines that will prove the wisdom of the administration.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) who preceded me said that the expenditure of the Dominion had largely increased. That is quite true. It is also true that when we were in opposition we condemned the expenditure of the then Conservative administration. But we not only condemned the expenditure ; we pointed out instances of sheer waste of public money. It is no argument to say that the expenditure has increased and to infer at once that this is conclusive proof of the extravagance of the government. This government has been spending more money it is true ; but the country has been growing and more expenditure has been necessary. Take any corporation or any firm in a large way of business, and you will find that their expenditure is very much larger than it was seven years ago. This government has done a business of $467,000,000, against a business of $239,000,000 seven years ago. It would be absurd to expect this increase in business to be effected without an increase of expenditure. When we were in opposition, we condemned the publie expenditure, which was then about $37,000,000 or $38,000,000. But we also pointed out specific cases in which public money might have been saved ? We pointed to the Curran bridge in Montreal, where $470,000 of the people's money was thrown away. We showed that we had here a Minister of Railways and Canals, a deputy Mr. CAMPBELL.
minister, a chief engineer and all the necessary staff, and yet, within telephone and telegraph communication, within 120 miles, of the city of Ottawa a work was carried out that cost the people $470,000 more than it should have cost. We pointed to the Tay Canal, where $500,000 of the people's money had been spent. We showed that it cost to operate that canal $3,000 a year and that the total receipts were $127.76. We pointed to the Langevin block, on which $400,000 was expended uselessly. We showed that the government had let a contract for that building, and that it was afterwards found that the contract was so loosely and carelessly drawn that the contractor was not obliged to put a roof on the building, and so a new contract had to be made for the. roof.
In that way we pointed out case after ease where the money of this country was squandered in many ways and enormous sums spent uselessly. If our Conservative friends could point to the same conditions to-day, if they could show where money is being wasted as we showed before 1896, then I think they could make a case against us. They are not justified in pointing to the increased expenditure when they know that when they left office they had started the deepening of the St. Lawrence and Welland canals, had let contracts for these works, and that it was necessary for this government to go on and complete them. If 1 remember coryectly, we have expended more than $11,000,000 in carrying out and completing work started under their regime. The Trent Valley canal was started under them-$1,000,000 were spent upon it, contracts were let, and it was absolutely necessary for the new government to go on and complete that work. Thus we have spent a great deal of money upon it. We have extended the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. That extension was fought and opposed at every stage in this House by our Conservative friends. It was called the Drummond County deal and the Drummond County steal, and all the opprobrious names they could think of. Now, realizing their mistake, they want to extend the Intercolonial Railway to Georgian bay. We wisely spent $1,000,000 or $1,500,000 in extending it to Montreal. The Intercolonial Railway before that stopped at Levis, although the great metropolis of Canada (was almost within a stone's throw of the end of the line. The Intercolonial Railway was obliged to take whatever rates the Grand Trunk would give them on freight that went to the maritime provinces, but immediately the line was extended to Montreal it was in direct competition with the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canada Atlantic, and all the enormous traffic that came down the Welland canal. In consequence the receipts of the Intercolonial Railway have more than doubled in the last seven years and are increasing year by year. It is true that we have spent a great deal

of money on the Intercolonial Railway, out that was absolutely necessary. The enormous development that took place in Sydney made it necessary that the road should be laid with heavier rails from Port Mulgrave to Sydney. That stretch of road had been laid with rails of only 45 pounds to the yard. It was absolutely necessary that a new steamer should be bought. The old ferry took over one car at a time and then came back and got another. That would do in Conservative times, when the country was standing still, but when the country began to move forward by leaps and bounds, when the life blood of this nation was running at a higher rate of speed than ever before, when new life permeated this whole Dominion, then we had to move forward. It was necessary to provide a steamer to carry trains across the Straits of Oan-so. It was necessary that that section of the road should be laid with heavy 90-pound rails, and this was done. The terminal facilities at Sydney were altogether too small, and the same conditions prevailed in Halifax and St. John. New cars had to be obtained, the bridges had to be strengthened, rails had to be relaid, locomotives had to be replaced, the little tu'penny-halfpenny- one-horse locomotives that could only haul half a dozen cars would do all right when this country was governed by the Tory party , but when a new party came in, then it was necessary that we should move forward with the times and improve our position. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway have spent millions of money in the last seven years in providing new cars, in increasing their locomotive equipment, in relaying tracks, in strengthening bridges and replacing wooden bridges with iron and steel structures. The Intercolonial had to do the same thing. We have spent large sums of money on the Intercolonial Railway, but to-day we are reaping the benefit from that expenditure. I believe that this expenditure has now almost ceased, and we shall reap a large revenue from the Intercolonial, I have no doubt, within the next few years.
Then the government has also expended a large amount for the construction of the Crow's Nest Pass Railway. The development taking place in the Kootenay district made it absolutely necessary that a line of railway should be extended into that country, and the Crow's Nest Pass road was built. The government had the choice of either building the road themselves or subsidizing the Canadian Pacific Railway for building it. It was thought that if the government built that road they would have a piece of road with no connections to the east or west, and would be absolutely at the dictation of the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other road or roads, in the matter of freight rates of freight they might get over it. Thus the government wisely concluded that it was better to subsidize the Canadian 145
Pacific Railway to build that line. But they took great care to protect the rights and interests of the people of Canada. They said to the Canadian Pacific Railway : You must give to the Dominion of Canada a fee simple to 50,000 acres of coal lands. The Dominion of Canada have to-day a deed in fee simple to 50,000 acres of the best coal lands there as a guarantee that the obligations of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be carried out. They stipulated, in order to avoid the discouragement or embarrassment to manufacturers or smelting works that might start there, that there should be no monopoly on coal. The government stipulated that coal should be furnished to those who required it at a fixed rate of $2 a ton at the pit's mouth, and, as a guarantee that they would carry that out, they were to deed to the government 50,000 acres of coal lands, so that if they should disregard their obligation, we have this enormous reservoir of coal which we can open up and so control the markets and the price. Not only that, but they stipulated that the Canadian Pacific Railway should give running powers to any other road that is now built or that may be built in Canada over the Crow's Nest Pass for all time .to come. As long as the sun shines and the rain falls that road will be under the qontrol of the Dominion of Canada, and the government can give running powers over it to any road upon terms to be settled by the Governor in Council. They also stipulated that the Canadian Pacific Railway should give reduced rates between the east and the west, and it was estimated that the concessions made by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the people of this Dominion would amount to between $600,000 and $700,000 every single year. That estimate was based on the amount of freight handled at that time, and, of eourse: the figures would be very much greater now7. In five years the people of Canada got back every single dollar of the subsidy given to the Crow's Nest Pass in the reduced rates on traffic both ways between the east and the west. These concessions will still go on all along the years, so that the bargain made by the government was a wise one. But, of course, it takes a considerable amount of money. We cannot have our cake and eat it, too ; but it was a wise thing to do, it was a wise expenditure, and I have always taken the position that I do not care what the expenditure is, $25,000,000, or $50,000,000, or $75,000,000 a year, so long as we get value for it. If it gives good returns to this country it is a wise expenditure. This government, by their wise administration, have been able to go on with great works, have been able to deepen the canals, to extend the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, to subsidize the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, to subsidize all the different railways running all over this Dominion and to construct public works necessary to the convenience and prosperity of the people in the mari-

time provinces. My hon., friend from Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) pointed to the fact that little wharfs and piers were built where there were very few settlers. It is the life and salvation of these fishermen down east that these wharfs shall be provided for them and the government have, by meeting the wishes of the people and providing all these necessary conveniences, aided, encouraged and increased the happiness of the people to a very great degree. Not only have they done that, but owing to the wise care which they have exercised in the management of the affairs of this country, notwithstanding the large expenditure they have made on the public works of this Dominion, in subsidizing railways, in deepening our canals, in extending the Intercolonial Eailway to Montreal, at the end of seven years we find the public debt of this Dominion $1,000,000 less than it was in 1890. Contrast that with the record of our Conservative friends. For the eighteen years they were in power they added $6,700,000 every single year to the debt of this Dominion. Not one single year passed by in the whole of the eighteen years during which they did not add $6,700,000 to the public debt and in the eighteen years that they were in power they increased the public debt by $118,000,000 while this government have been able to carry on the public works and improve the conditions of the people, increase their comfortsf facilitate and improve transportation and open up the canals, doing all this work and at the same time relieving the people at the end of seven years by reducing the debt to the extent of $1,000,000. This is a record that any government might be proud of. I am sure it is a record that the people of this Dominion will look upon as one of the best records that was ever made by any government. It is a record I am sure will meet with the approval of the people and when the elections come on, be it sooner or be it later, I have no doubt that from one end of this broad Dominion to the other the people will say: Well done, good and faithful servants ; enter ye into another seven years of power.

Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry that we on this side of the House are not able to please hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the length of* our speeches. If an hon. gentleman rises, on this side of the House to make a lengthyj speech some hon. gentlemen opposite is sure to say that the time of the House is being wasted. But the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Campbell) found fault rather with the shortness of the speeches which have been delivered on this side of the House. He evi-dent'lv wants quantity rather than quality, and I am sure the House will agree with me when I say that he has set a worthy example in that respect during the last hour and a half. It is true that the hon. gen-Mr. CAMPBELL.
tleman went over a great deal of ground, and I am sure that hon. members who have been longer in this House than I have been, must admit that they have heard a great deal of that speech once or twice before ; an hon. gentleman beside me says six times. The chief argument throughout the hon. gentleman's speech was, that, this country being exceedingly prosperous, the government in power at the present time are entitled to the credit for that prosperity. Last night we had an excelient speech from the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd). But that hon. gentleman was more modest. He was willing to give Providence credit for at least some small portion of the prosperity we have had in this country during the last few years. But, the hon. member for West York was not at all satisfied with the statement of the hon. member for South Brant because he was willing apparently to take credit on behalf of the government for all of the bountiful harvests that we have had for the last five years. The money value of these harvests, or of the good crops that we have had during the last five years, I am informed on good authority, is something like $500,000,000 greater than it was in the previous seven years. I do not know whether the hon. member for West York is willing or not to say in public that the government has had anything to do with the raising of these magnificent crops. But, it is evident from the tone of his remarks that he thinks it has. The hon. gentleman, as usual, takes a great deal of credit to the government because of the increase in our exports and imports and he wishes to gauge the prosperity of the country on that basis. In regard to our exports and imports he lays a considerable amount of stress upon our exports of agricultural implements. He scores the government that preceded this one on the ground that during the time it was in control of the affairs of this country our agricultural implement manufacturers were not exporting large quantities of agricultural implements while at the present time they were exporting to the extent of $2,228,000 a year. The hon. gentleman might have gone a little farther. He might have stated, if he had desired to be absolutely fair, that in 1896 we did export $593,464 worth of agricultural implements. The business of manufacturing agricultural implements in this country only got on its feet some twelve or fifteen years ago. After the national policy had been put in operation the effect was immediately manifest. The larger proportion of the agricultural implements used in Canada were made in this country and the manufacturers got into the position of being able to export a large quantity of these products. This export in 1896 amounted to no less than $593,464. But, that was not all. At that time the manufacturers of these implements gave employment to our own good Canadians who made almost all of the imple-

ments that we used in this country. We imported only $304,000 worth. What is happening to-day ? Although we exported $2,228,000 worth we imported $3,255,000 worth under this magnificent tariff which is now in operation. Of course that goes to swell the export and import total and the hon. gentleman takes credit for that condition of affairs. I am sure the people are not satisfied with the fact that three and a quarter million dollars worth of agricultural implements were made across the line that should have been made in Canada. The hon. gentleman who spoke previously, said that a protective tariff of twenty per cent had brought these large factories to the city of Hamilton that are locating there at the present time. I am bound to say that even a twenty per cent protective tariff will in some cases bring industries into this country-not in all cases. Here is an example. For a great many years the International Harvester Company, the McCormicks, the Deerings, and other large manufacturers of agricultural implements on the other side of the line consented to pay that twenty per cent duty, brought their implements into this country and sold them in competition with those of our own manufacturers. It is true that they charged a little higher prices, but twenty per cent when the implement is invoiced at not more than $50 is not a very serious item and they were able not only to maintain their position on equal terms with the Canadian manufacturers but they were able to retain a foothold in the market in the hope relying upon the assurances of hon. gentlemen opposite that when they got into power they would have a free trade government or that they would have unrestricted reciprocity and that they would then be able to bring their implements in free. But, when this government had been in power a number of years and when these manufacturers found that these hon. gentlemen were not prepared to carry out the principles upon which they had appealed to the people previously to the election, they came to the conclusion that both political parties in this country were determined to maintain some sort of protective tariff, and that the only thing they could do was to come across the line. But, this was not until after the lapse of a long number of years and until after we had imported into this country scores of millions of dollars worth of these agricultural implements the manufacture of which had given employment in the United States to thousands of men. At last this low tariff brought this industry to this country. What would have been the consequence if instead, a twenty-five or thirty per cent tariff had been put on and that tariff had been maintained all these years and that the Liberal leaders had not preached free trade 1 The implement manufacturers on the other side of the line would not have believed from the assurances of these hon. gentlemen 145*
while in opposition that there might be a change in the policy of this country but they would have known that protection was the fixed policy of this country with the result that these industries would have been brought into this country fifteen years ago instead of now.
Had that been done then, we would have been saved from sending out of this country millions of dollars in capital, and thousands of Canadians to work in the factories of the United States. The hon. gentleman claimed that these industries were brought to Canada on account of the present tariff, but he did not say that it is absolutely the same tariff now as under the Conservative regime so far as agricultural implements are concerned. The hon. gentleman tried to show that our prosperity was in some way due to the Minister of Agriculture, who, being a horny-handed son of toil, and knowing everything about agriculture, set to work to revolutionize matters when he took charge of the department. Well, one of the first things the Minister of Agriculture did was to go to Washington with the Hon. John Dryden to induce the Americans to do away with the cattle quarantine. That was a wonderful accomplishment of the minister. The Conservative government maintained a quarantine against American cattle for years, so that Canadian live cattle might be allowed to enter into the United kingdom. It was admitted by the English government that our cattle were free from disease, but the embargo was maintained as a matter of protection to the British farmer. However, when Mr. Fisher came into power, he got the cattle quarantine between Canada and the United States removed, and so he gave up all hope for ever of having our cattle admitted into the English market. Last year we exported to the United States 10,432 head of cattle, valued at $292,000, or an average of $27.90 cents per head. Well, any farmer who would send an animal worth only $27.90 to be fattened in the United States is not a good farmer. The good farmer is the farmer who will fatten his cattle at home. Did not this government remove the duty on American corn, to compel the Canadian farmer not to grow corn himself, but to buy foreign corn in order to fatten his cattle ? However that may be, a few farmers sent cattle to the United States last year to the value of $292,000. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) did not say a word about the fact that last year we imported $497,000 worth of American cattle into Canada. The hon. gentleman is quite satisfied to let the Americans send in half a million dollars worth of cattle, if he can only find a market in the United States for $292,000 worth of calves and lean animals. But, our cattle trade with Great Britain is not a trade in lean cattle and calves. It is a trade in fat cattle, as will be seen from

the fact that last year we exported to the British market 161,170 head worth $10,842,000, or an average of $67 a head. These were fat cattle fattened on Canadian farms, and exported to the British market in their finished state, as they should be exported by good farmers. Gentleman on the other side of the House boast year after year that they have taken down the cattle quarantine regulations so as to enable us to send $292,000 of calves and lean cattle to the United States, forgetting to state that American cattle to double that value were imported here. What have they done to open up the British market for our cattle ? Nothing. What have they done to open up the German market for our own produce ? A few years ago we did a trade with Germany amounting to $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 worth of agricultural products more than we do to-day. But that trade has disappeared. I will not say the government did wrong in putting the surtax on German goods, but I do say that if they claim credit because we sell $292,000 worth of cattle to the United States, they must also have the discredit of destroying that large and profitable market which we had in Germany.
