What I want to know is, if it is right and proper, and I say it is, that the1 manufacturers of this country should be protected to the extent of 28 per cent, wh y is it not equally right and proper that the farmer, who toils day and night, who earns his money qs hardly as any other people in this country, should also have protection ? I know that hon. gentlemen opposite will

smile and sneer, and say, of what advantage is it to put a duty on wheat, cheese or butter ? Do we not export enormous quantities of these products, and does not the Liverpool price fix the price in Canada ? Then what is the use of putting a duty upon them ? It would not raise the price a single cent. I say if it does not, put it on ; it cannot do anybody any harm. But I fancy if would have the effect of giving the farmers of this country their home market for these $5,756,000 worth of agricultural products which are now imported, instead of their taking the chances of getting their products damaged and spoiled by sending them across the Atlantic. The home market is the best market. Almost everybody will admit that. Hon. gentlemen opposite, who used to sneer at the idea of a home market for the farmers, are now coming to the conclusion that it is their best market. I want to preserve this home market for the farmers, and it can be preserved for them, by giving them as high a duty on their products as is imposed on things they have to buy. That is fair, surely.
Let us discuss some of these items separ-; ately. I want to know why the farmers, of this country cannot supply this market with butter, cheese, lard, pork and grain products. Then, I want to speak of another class of goods that are luxuries. However much we may disagree with hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to other things ; however strong protectionists we may be, and however honestly we may hold our coni victions, however consistent we may have been during the last twenty-five years with regard to protection, and however inconsistent these hon. gentlemen may be in that matter; we can, I believe, all agree on one thing ; protectionists, free traders and revenue tariff men will agree that luxuries should be taxed a little higher than the necessaries of life ; and a large proportion of these agricultural products that come to this country are luxuries, and as such, they ought to pay more than 28 per cent. They ought to pay at least 35 per cent, which is a common rate of duty in our tariff. Just consider that we bring in seventy-nine carloads of these green tomatoes which our market-gardeners around our cities and town could grow. They are a, class of men who are industrious, frugal, persevering and hard working. Our market-gardeners and fruit growers are two classes of men who perhaps earn their money as hardly as any other class in the country. Their productions are subject to droughts, frosts, floods and all manner of insect pests, and they have to be continually on the fight. Theirs is a business that calls forth the highest kind of intelligence, and they are a class of citizens who form the backbone of the great agricultural class. Their life is one that necessarily calls forth the high
est qualities in a man. These men employ a great many men In their business. This government are paying out millions of dollars a year in bonuses.
I think we have paid up to date over $4,000,000 in direct bounties to establish industries in this country. What are these paid for ? Is it not to give employment in this country ? I think that is the great object; and, if so, there is no class among farmers that employ more men than the market-gardeners and fruit growers. They employ ten times the number of men to the square mile that any other class does outside of manufacturers. These are a class of men who ought to be encouraged. They are engaged in an occupation which is particularly hazardous. They ought, therefore, to have at any rate as much protection as is accorded to other industries, namely, 28 per cent. But, as a matter of fact, they are only getting an average of 18 per cent. But the tomatoes I have referred to are luxuries and ought to be subject to a higher duty than the average. They ought to pay 35 per cent or even 45 per cent; but they have to pay only 19J per cent. No wonder the market-gardeners are complaining every year that they are not properly treated by this government. The wonder is that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) has not been more powerful-has not raised his sturdy voice in council and before the Minister of Finance from time to time on! their behalf. I am sure that if the hon. gentleman had raised his influential voice on this question in the manner he has done on other questions, he would have convinced the government that 19i per cent protection is not sufficient for the market-gardener. Go over the various items which the market-gardeners grow, and you will find that the
i.uties are below the average and that these gentlemen have a just grievance against] the government.
I might take up another department ol these agricultural products-the fruit industry. I find that we imported into this country 28,391 barrels of apples, 200 carloads, and exported some 20,000 carloads. No doubt hon. gentlemen opposite will say : if you export in such large quantities, what gcod would it do you to put a higher duty on the small quantity you import ? It would not raise the price a cent. Well, let us have the duty in any case. We will then get the market and that is what our farmers want. What they want is a market at their doors for the 28,000 barrels which they now have to send across the ocean, but which would be consumed at home if these 28,000 barrels of American apples did not come in. They would have that much less to send across in the magnificent cold storage system, of which hon. gentlemen opposite boast so much and to which I shall refer later. Of dried apples we imported no less than eight carloads, and I suppose we had a thousand carloads last

goods out of the country. I think if even a small portion of this money were spent upon our great waterways and in the development of that system of transportation, far better results could be obtained than by the expenditure of this enormous amount on the scheme proposed by the government. We find that, in shipping grain from the upper lakes to Montreal, we have an advantage over New York of not less than li cents per bushel. But we find also that, when grain has to be transhipped at Montreal for Liverpool, we lose that 11 cents per bushel. The St. Lawrence route, though shorter than that by New York, is not developed. There are many hindrances, many obstacles, all of which I believe, could be removed by an energetic government. When we are compelled to pay at the port of Montreal so high a rate on goods brought down through our magnificent system of canals, which by the way was inaugurated and nearly completed under a Conservative administration -the advantage which' the country gains from its enterprise and great expenditure is neutralized. I find that last year we exported from the port of Montreal $70,000,000 worth of goods. For instance we exported 24,272,390 bushels of wheat, and on that we were compelled to pay 11 cents a bushel more than would have been paid for the carriage of wheat from Boston or New York. That amounts to $364,085. I. find that we exported from that port 21,182,840 pounds of butter and on that we paid 5 shillings a ton more than we would pay from Boston or New York. That amounted to $12,709.
We exported from Montreal 184,494,040 tons of cheese. We paid on that 3s. and 9d. a ton more than we would pay from Boston or New York. That amounted to $83,022.
Of apples we shipped 800,987 ban-els and paid 10 cents a barrel extra on them. This cost us $80,098. That makes a total of $539,914.
At the same ratio, if we took the balance of exports from Montreal and found the in crease-1 have no doubt that the freight rates were in the same proportion-we will find that the total excess freights amounted to $829,920. As the price we received for these export goods, to a large extent, sets the price of the goods sold in this country, there is no doubt that we lost a good deal more than this. It may be safely said that we lost $1,000,000 because the route from Montreal out past the banks of Newfoundland is not in the condition it ought to be in. First of all, the ships have to go slow a large part of the way, and cannot make good time. Then occasionally wrecks take place, and we have in consequence high insurance rates. The port of Montreal has large harbour dues, and ail these things combined with others that might he mentioned go to make up the reason why our steamers have to charge a higher rate of freight from that port notwithstanding that many of them are bonused. We pay out annually Mr. E. D. SMITH.
something between $100,000 and $150,000 to these steamers simply to come to Montreal. Ostensibly this is paid for the carrying of mail matter, but we only sent about thirty-nine tons of mail matter to the old country in the last year, ancl if you quadrupled the rates on ordinary freight the freight on this mail matter would toe only $1,500 ; yet we paid $150,000 to one line of steamers to go to Montreal and St. John, so that we ought to have the very best .service there. Some people say the insurance people have no right to charge the high rates that they do ; that they are discriminating unjustly against our routes. Whether that is so or not I cannot isay, but on looking at the report of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for the past year X find that a considerable number of shipwrecks occurred on the St. Lawrence, and a large portion of those shipwrecks occurred through faults that might have been prevented if the Minister of Marine had in the last three years devoted his energies to thoroughly improving this St. Lawrence route, and if a proper pilotage system had prevailed, most of these shipwrecks could have been averted. Let me read the result of the examination by the commissioner, Mr. O. G. Y. Spain, into some of these ship wrecks,- and What he says in regard to the reasons why they occurred. I come first to the wreck of the steamer ' Oarrigan Head ' :
This British steamship grounded opposite No. 3 lightship, Lake St. Peter, River St. Lawrence, on April 24, 1903. A ,formal investigation was held into the casualty at the harbour commissioners' office, Montreal, and the finding of the court was as follows
That the captain was not to blame for the disaster. That the officer of the watch was not. to blame for the disaster. That the quartermaster carried out the orders of the pilot. That pilot Angers was not to blame. That the casualty was due to the buoys being out of place.
Why were the buoys out of place ? Why is there not a proper patrol over this river to see that the buoys are always in place 1 Surely it is the duty of the Minister of Marine and of the government to see that the buoys are in place. Had this been done the wreck would not have occurred, insurance rates would not be so high, and we would not have to pay such high freight rates on our produce.
Then there is the wreck of the steamship ' Iberian ' :
This British steamship grounded on the south side of the channel, near Isle aux Raisins, River St. Lawrence, on June 6, 1903, and at a formal investigation into the causes which led to the casualty, held at the harbour commissioners' office, Montreal, the court found :-
That nothing in the ship or her equipment contributed toward the accident.
That the conditions of the weather prevailing at the time of the casualty were favour-

.able, bat navigation was rendered difficult, though not unsafe, by smoke from bush fires, which limited the distance the buoys were visible to about half a mile.
That proper precautions were taken with regard to speed, the ship steaming about four (4) knots per hour

_ The fog signals were not perfect. There is an opportunity for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to improve that route by establishing some more fog signals. These gentlemen are experienced, and it is their opinion that the route was not properly marked. Then, there is the case of the barque ' Sardhana.' The report of the commissioner appointed to investigate the wreck ot this vessel states :
That the aids to navigation-in so far as the fog-signal at Point des Monts iS concerned -were inefficient ; the evidence of various Witnesses going to show that it was impossible to hear the fog-signal, even after the vessel stranded, within a mile and a-half of the lighthouse.
These are the results of the examinations of a few of the wrecks that occurred, and they go to show plainly that the fault lies with the government and with the minister who is in charge of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It shows that he has not devoted his energies during all these long years to the improvement of this great rente, this route by which almost all the products originating west from the port of Montreal find their outlet to the sea. The evidence of these gentlemen appointed by tbe government themselves goes to prove that most of these accidents could have been prevented if proper signals and buoys had been provided. These are some of the things that I desire to call to the attention of the House, and I say that it is the duty of the government to bend their energies in this direction so as to make the St Lawrence route so safe that it will be as easy and as cheap to carry goods bv that route as by any other route1 from the Atlantic coast. There are other things that go to make that route cheap and safe. A large portion of the goods that we send from the port of Montreal are perishable goods. Three of our large exports are butter, cheese and apples. All of these are perishable products and require tbe best of care. It does not matter how much education our butter makers may have, it does not matter how much money may be spent upon educating our factory men to make the best butter that it is possible to make, it does not matter how much energy our farmers may bi mg to tbe work of producing good butter if you cannot carry it across the ocean m perfect condition. From $3,000,000 to $o.000,000 of our butter goes across the ocean and finds a market there. Most of it is sent m cold storage, and if we were to judge from the laudatory remarks which the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House made, we would come to the conclusion that the cold storage system as it at present exists is the most perfect in the world. We would imagine that every ship that sails from the port of Montreal is equipped with cold storage chambers that Mr. E. D. SMITH.
will carry every pound of butter across the Atlantic and land it in perfect condition in England where it will bring the highest prices. The cold storage system was inaugurated by the Hon. Mr. Montague when he was Minister of Agriculture, not at all, as the hon. member for West York tried to make this House believe, by the present hon. Minister of Agriculture. That system then inaugurated has no doubt become a great deal better than it was eight oi ten years ago. It would be a curious thing if after eight years of experience the Minister of Agriculture, with the able men lie has in bis employ, with the funds of the government at his disposal with which to equip these steamers as they are equipped except partially by the steamship companies, though the steamers sailing out of Boston and New York provide their own equipment, should not be able to carry out a better system of cold storage than that which previously prevailed. It would be dtrange if there was no improvement. There has been improvement. It would be strange indeed, after the long experience we have had with this very simple matter of cold storage, a thing that has been in operation in Australia and other portions of the world, which has been utilized for the carriage of perishable products to Great Britain for twenty years, a system which is in operation in all our cities and towns where you can place goods in cold storage and maintain them for months, if the government, with ample funds at their disposal, were not able to have a perfect system of cold stoiage. I am sure you will agree witb me that it is not very much to their credit that they have failed to perfect that system. Last year the hon. minister promised a thermograph record would be placed in every one of the chambers in ocean vessels for carrying perishable products. I find, however, that there are only 199 thermo-gi aph records taken, 155 in cold storage chambers, 32 in cooled chambers, and 12 in ordinary storage. Then I find the hon. minister in his report saying that a number of these boats carried butter in cold storage chambers at a temperature, not that which the hon. minister prescribes, but a temperature very far away from that which any experienced man knows they ought to maintain. The hon. minister maintained last year in his report 20 degrees as the proper temperature for the carriage of butter. Tbe butter shippers ask for a temperature of ten degrees. You would think that the boats would carry the butter below 32, the freezing point, but I find in the bon. minister's report that no less than nine boats carried it at an average temperature, not on a single day, but at an average temperature of over 32 degrees, and some of them averaged as higl^ as 40 degrees, 43 degrees, 36 degrees, 35 degrees, 39 degrees, 38 degrees, and so on.

I find on turning up the thermograph records that a very large number carried butter to London at temperatures ranging from below 32 degrees to 45 and 50 degrees. I find that the ' Iona,' sailing September 5, carried apples at a temperature of from 66 to 45 degrees. How could you expect apples, or pears, or any perishable fruits to be landed on the British market after a journey of fourteen days at a temperature of 45 degrees to 66 degrees, confined in a close cold storage chamber ? Then, I find that on the ' Hibernian,' sailing August 22, there was a temperature of from 68 to 42 degree ; on the ' Hurona,' sailing July 12, a temperature of from 50 to 40 degrees ; on the ' Devona,' June 28, a temperature of from 37 to 38 degrees, on the ' Iona,' June 13, a temperature of from 42 and 32 degrees, on the ' Kildona,' a temperature of from 42 and 29 degrees, during their respective voyages across the ocean. All these vessels carried butter at the temperatures which I have mentioned except the first two, which carried apples. Then, taking the Liverpool service, I find that the ' Ionian ' had a temperature of from 41 to 38 degrees, that the ' Kensington ' had a temperature of from 45 degrees to 30 degrees, and that a number of other steamers had temperatures very much higher than they ought to have been for butter. This goes to show that the cold storage system that the hon. member for West York lauded so highly is not the perfect success that the House might have been led to believe if they had accepted that hon. gentleman's remarks as representing accurately the facts of the case. I am not going to say there was not a very large number of boats which carried butter at a proper temperature. Certainly the large majority of them carried it at a proper temperature and there is a very great improvement in this respect, but the point I wish to make is : That after these long years of experience it is astonishing that there should have been a single cargo go out from the port of Montreal shipped in cold storage not carried at a proper temperature. Every one of these cargoes can be carried at a proper temperature. It is only a matter of looking after them properly. It is not that it can not be done, it is simply a matter that requires somebody to attend to it. There should be some body to keep urging it upon the steamship owners, who, I have no doubt would be quite willing if it were continually brought to their attention to see to it that a temperature was maintained to carry butter in a proper condition.
The result is that our exports of butter dropped from between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 worth to between $3,000,000 or $4,000,-, 000 worth. That is largely due to the fact that a great portion of our butter landed in England in a poor condition. Of course the blame was laid on the butter makers. My
experience is that if anything goes wrong the blame is put on the producer. He is a long distance off; he is not in parliament to defend himself ; he is not in the public eye, and so he is an easy mark for blame. Now, I doubt that the butter producer is responsible for this. I believe that the butter makers of Canada, with their experience) and intelligence, are able tq put up butter in as good shape as the people of any country in the world. I have no reason whatever to doubt that these cold storage chambers on the steamers with a temperature of 35 or 40 degrees instead of 20 degrees, are the sole and only cause why Canadian butter arrived in a mouldy condition on the English market, and why our exports of butter have decreased by millions of dollars. We were promised at the outset that this government would do a great deal for fruit-growers, and they started in a feeble manner to imitate the policy of Dr. Montague when Minister of Agriculture. Dr. Montague held that it was the duty of the government to see that Canadian fruit and butter were properly looked after in transit, and he could not understand why, if Australian fruit and butter could be carried through the tropics half way around the world in good condition, Canadian fruit and butter should not reach the English market in like manner. Dr. Montague experimented with butter. He bought a certain quantity of butter at 20 cents per pound, sold it in the English market, and proved that Canadian butter could compete with any butter in the world. Our butter export trade which was then practically nothing has since amounted to $5,000,000 and over some seasons. These experiments of Dr. Montague cost the country about $1,000, and I can well remember how the Liberals of that day loudly condemned the Conservative Minister of Agriculture for making this useless expenditure. But when they came to power, as they did in many other cases, they adopted the Conservative policy and swallowed themselves. They started experimental fruit shipments to the old country. They have been at it for eight years, and still without success. Let me point out that the Bartlett pear, one of our best pears, is a fruit that we ought to be able to ship in cold storage. I have kept them in cold storage in this country for several months, and I have taken them out in such sound and hard condition, that I have been obliged to put them in a warm rcom for a few days to ripen them sufficiently for use in the canning factory. Now, after eight years experimenting, the Minister of Agriculture is yet unable to have these Bartlett pears sent to England in good condition. We are voting here thousands and thousands of dollars to the minister and surely he should have sufficient control over his cold storage, to so regulate it that this

fruit might be carried for an ocean voyage of ten days and landed in sound condition on the English market. Yet, last year 1 believe there were only two carloads of these pears sent across, and both were an entire loss. In addition to apples, practically the only thing which the fruit-growers can ship in cold storage chambers at the present time, are some of our late fall pears that will keep in good condition in any old sort of place. Hr. Fisher and other gentlemen in the neighbourhood of Burlington have been shipping these pears for a number of years without cold storage, and have been making money out of the business. We can keep our pears in good condition in our own cold storage chambers and yet the Minister of Agriculture, to whom the member for West York gives so much credit and who has costly apparatus at his disposal, cannot arrange that they may be kept for the ocean voyage of ten days. But, Sir, only a comparatively small portion of our perishable goods require to go in cold storage. We export $20,000,000 worth of cheese, and that does not require cold storage. All that it needs is that the air should be constantly changed and kept as cool as the outside air of the ocean. The same thing applies to shipments of apples. On this side of the House I urged on the Minister of Agriculture years ago, that all that is required for cheese and apples was to have the steamer holds properly ventilated, I showed him the enormous loss that we were sustaining by the neglect of this precaution, but he did not heed us. It was at last ascertained, when we came to make a milder kind of cheese that it would not carry under the old conditions, and at last the commissioner appeared before the Agricultural Committee one day, and stated that our cheese had been so damaged during the previous year by being carried in ill ventilated steamship holds, that it had received a black eye in the old country, and he prophesied that for the following year our cheese exports would be reduced by $3,000,000. I thought that in all probability he was right, and I watched the matter closely, and true enough next year our exports of cheese instead of increasing by one and a half million dollars as had been usual, decreased by one million dollars, so that we lost about two and a half million dollars on our cheese exports for that year. I on this side of the House had cautioned the Minister of Agriculture year after year that this would happen; I told him the farmers of Ontario were losing at least a million dollars a year on their apple shipments on account of this fact, but the Minister of Agriculture did nothing. He only woke up when he heard from his commissioner. The minister sent a circular to the steamship owners asking them to Mr. E. D. SMITH.
provide that the holds should be ventilated.
The hon. minister thought to take a little credit to himself, and what did he do ? He came to this House and asked for a vote of $40,000-not to ventilate the steamers. That was a simple matter. He did not require any vote for that. All that was required was for him to point out to the steamship companies the necessity of the case, and to tell them that if they did not ventilate their holds, and let the agents of the government see that they were properly ventilated, he would report and publish the fact. That would not have cost the country a cent. But that did not suit the hon. gentleman. These hon. gentlemen opposite have come to regard money of so little account, that unless they can come to this House and ask for a vote of $100,000 or some other large amount, they do not think they can do anything for the people. So the hon. minister asked for $40,000, and that vote has been repeated several times, to assist the steamship companies to fit up their steamers with cool air chambers and a refrigerating plant and thus reduce the temperature below that of the ocean air. I had grave doubts at the time whether this would work out as the hon. minister seemed to think it would. I rather imagined that the steamship people, having to pay at any rate a portion of the cost of fitting up the steamers, and having to set apart a considerable amount of space for the refrigerating plant would have to charge a considerable extra rate for the use of them. The minister assured us that the rate would be the same. So the money was voted and the chambers were fitted up in a number of these steamers ; and what do we find ? We find that the temperatures in these cool air chambers are just about the same as in chambers which are properly ventilated. I find, for instance, that on the ' Cervona, ' the temperature of the cold air chamber was 62 to 54, and on the * ' Pretorian' with ordinary ventilated storage, 65 to 56 ; almost the same temperature. On the ' Kil-dona ' with cool air temperature 56 to 58 ; on the ' Ionian ' without cool air, the temperature was 45 to 62. I might read a dozen or so of reports of temperatures of steamers fitted up with cool air chambers : but I could only read twelve with regard to the ordinary storage, because these were all the hon. gentleman had recorded and it would be found that there is very little difference in this temperature in the cool air chamber and that in a properly ventilated chamber. It was pointed out to the minister last year that the only way to secure the object in view was to have his agents at Montreal, put a thermograph into every storage apartment, and have his agents on the other side examine them and report. This would not cost the country a single cent, as the bon. gentleman has his agents now. In order to see that the holds

are properly ventilated, he should have a compartment on deck or somewhere when the exact temperature of the ocean air would be recorded ; and if the record of that corresponded exactly with the record in the holds where the cargoes were, he would know that the fans were going; otherwise he would not know. It is all very well for him to have his agents go and see that the steamers are provided with the necessary apparatus ; but it is another thing to know that the apparatus is working all the way across the ocean. If it is not, it will not produce any result. In response to a question which I put to the minister last year, he promised that in every one of the holds carrying perishable cargo there would be a thermograph, but I find that they were only put into twelve ; but fortunately even these twelve show the advantage of them. I have examined the record of vessels going from Montreal on the same date and arriving on the other side at the same time. If the fans had been going and the holds had been ventilated, they would have shown exactly the same temperatures. I find that the ' Livonia ' had temperatures ranging from 45 to 60, and for five days the temperature was 50 or lower. I venture to say that in that case the fans were going and the ventilating apparatus was in operation. At the temperature which prevailed during those five days, you could carry summer apples, pears, or any other perishable cargo that goes from this country to the other side, except perhaps butter, and I do not know but you could carry that in a temperature of from 45 to 50, if you were sure of having it all the time. What do I find with regard to the 'Tritonia' that went at the same time ? She never showed less temperature than 60, and that only when loading, when the ' Livonia ' was about from 57 to 60. The * Tritonia ' showed a rise to 68 at about the same time as the ' Livonia ' showed from 45 to 50, and the temperature rose gradually until it reached 73, when the vessel was across to the other side ; whereas the ' Livonia ' never got above 55, a difference of from 15 to 18 degrees during the whole voyage. This is exactly the result which I wanted the minister to prove. There is the proof that it is absolutely necessary to take some steps to see that these steamers are ventilated. All you have to do is to put a thermograph, which costs $10, into each apartment which carries perishable goods and to put another on the deck. These thermographs will last a number of years, and by their use we could secure absolutely safe carriage for all our apples and cheese across the ocean. But that did not suit the hon. minister. He must put cool air apartments on the steamers at a cost of $100,000. and what has been the result ? That of 2,000,000 barrels of apples exported last year only 8,000 barrels were carried in cool air chambers, and that of 229,000,000 pounds of
cheese exported only about 3,000,000 pounds were carried in cool air chambers, that is, one cheese in seventy-five. Why was this 7 Because the shippers found that where the ordinary storage is well ventilated, they can carry cheese and apples across in as perfect condition as in the cool air chambers that cost the country $100,000 and in which shippers have to pay 36 cents a barrel extra on apples and ten shillings a ton extra on cheese. The shippers therefore will not ship in them, because they can get as good service without paying these extra charges. Since a large number of steamships have found it to be in their own interest to provide proper ventilation, these cool air chambers are neglected and the $100,000 is thrown away. This service, for which the people have to pay an enormously increased cost, is not required if the minister would do what he is asked to do by members on this side of the House. If the hon, member who preceded me had devoted a little more of his energies in this direction, he would have been of more value to his constituents. That shows $920 realized more on a thousand barrels landed in the condition in which those sent on the ' Ionian ' were landed than would be realized on a similar quantity shipped by the ' Lake Champlain.' What does that mean ? That would mean on our exports of apples last year alone to the old country, some 2,000,000 barrels, a million dollars ; and 2,000,000 barrels is only a small portion of the products of this country. According to the Bureau of Statistics and Industry, the apple crop of Ontario alone was 50,000,000 bushels. If the price at Liverpool sets the price in this country-as no doubt it does to a very large extent on No. 1 at any rate and to some extent on No. 2-this million dollars would only represent a small portion of the loss. This is a matter of paramount importance. I do not say that a million dollars loss occurred on the apples we shipped, but I say that if they were carried in the conditions in which they were carried on the ' Lake Champlain '-and that was the condition almost in every boat before these ships were ventilated-that would have been our loss. That only shows what can be achieved by a proper system of ventilation upon these boats. I think I have talked long enough. I think that the government could do a great deal, if they liked, for the people of this country, and I have pointed out two things they ought to do. The cargoes to which I am just referring were carried last season, 1903.
In referring to the enormous prosperity of the country during the past year, the hon. gentleman who preceded me found of course, as do all the speakers on the opposite side, a great deal of comfort in the great expansion of our exports and imports, and they take credit to themselves to a very great extent for this expansion. In this connection, the hon. gentleman might have mentioned the article of binder twine, for instance. Last year I find that we imported 14,204,000 pounds of binder twine. Before these hon, gentlemen came into power, we imported 3,364,000 pounds. What does that mean ? It means simply that under the late administration we manufactured all our own binder twine except the small amount of 3,000,000 pounds, whereas now we are importing the larger portions. But of course that 14,000,000 pounds imported swells the trade and navigation returns. It keeps up the figures of trade and Mr. E. D. SMITH.
commerce, but none the less it threw out of employment a large number of Canadians. Hon. gentlemen opposite however do not take this into consideration. They do not seem to think it is of any moment that a large number of Canadians have not found employment. They say the country asl prosperous and the people busily employed. But, Sir, if that be the case, to what is it due ? It is due simply to the fact that the policy which was inaugurated by the Conservative party has, to a very large extent, been left alone. Why have our large industries prospered if it be not because the protection they enjoyed in the past has been continued ? But where are our binder twine factories and our barbed wire factories ? These are industries that the hon. gentlemen opposite did meddle with and these have disappeared. All the industries which are flourishing to-day are flourishing, not because of what these hon. gentlemen did. but because of what they did not do. And what about the industries that they did meddle with ? I have mentioned two, but I might mention others ? I might mention the woollen industry, in respect of which they partially carried out their promise of free trade, revenue tariff and so on, which they had been promulgating for eighteen years, and what was the result ? Last year we imported $13,516,915 worth of wol-len goods, whereas in 1897 we only imported $7,125,148 worth. There was an increase in our imports of over $6,000,000, which of course made the trade and navigation returns look bigger. But these hon. gentlemen found out that after all to swell the trade and navigation returns was not the best policy. They found out that the platform laid down by the Conservative party twenty-five years ago of adequate protection to our native industries is the only policy under which these industries will thrive. They found that, whenever they interfered with that policy, whenever they attempted to carry out the promises and fulfil the pledges they had been making for eighteen years, while they increased the trade and navigation returns, they injured and demolished our industries. And so it has come to pass that, whereas eight years ago practically no hon. gentlemen of the other side would dare on the public platform to avow themselves protectionists, we find them now, one by one and two by two, coming forward frankly as believers in the protectionist doctrine. This session we find the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) openly avowing himself an out-and-out protectionist. Last year he made a speech which abundantly showed that he was a protectionist, but he took care not to avow it. The year before that he made a speech which was not quite so strongly protectionist as the one of last year. And so, year by year, they are showing themselves more and more convinced that the policy of the Conservative party is the policy for this country. Even

If the hon. minister had taken the advice of members on this side, he would not have reduced those duties so low as to make this late increase necessary. Had he taken that advice we should not have imported $13,000,000 of woollen goods ; the figures in our trade and navigation return would not have been so large, but we should have had woollen mills in full operation that are closed to-day, and hundreds of operatives at work in Canada that to-day are out of employment. We should have had an industry thriving that is seriously injured to-day, and will take a long time to revive even with the protection he now at. this late hour affords it. But it is a consolation to us to know that the platform that we on this side have advocated for twenty-seven years, ever since 1878 and before, is at last recognized by hon. members opposite as the policy for this country. It is true that, not believing in that policy, they do not carry it out scientifically. How could you expect them to ? How can you expect men to carry out efficiently a policy that they adopt, not from conviction, but as a matter of political expediency ? The men to carry out a policy are the men who believe in it thoroughly. And, until the people of this country come to the conclusion that they had better put the Conservative party in power, they will never have a protective policy carried out in its entirety. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken many steps in our direction ; I prophesy that it will not be many years before they come a step further. Their adoption of our policy, as 1 said before, is a matter of congratulation to the country and of satisfaction to us But however efficacious it may be in keeping these hon. gentlemen in power, however large the number of the votes it may secure for them, it is a matter of congratulation for us that at last they have come to believe in the policy that we have so long believed in and so strongly advocated. But, as I have said, they must come a step further. I trust that the Finance Minister will take that step even before the close of this session. I have pointed out how our farmers are suffering, and I need not say that the farmers have a right to be treated in as fair, as generous and as liberal a manner as any other class. The hon. Minister of Finance has an opportunity-for this session is not yet closed-to right the wrong under which they labour. I am sure that the hon. gentleman, knowing that he is not infallible, will be glad of the opportunity to change his
mind ; and I trust that before this session is over he will concede to the farmers, the fruit-growers and gardeners of this country the protection which, in view of the importance of their industry, they well deserve.
